ask: Which of the following describes the business processes side of change management?

options.t: Tracking every edit to a file and who made it
options.why: That is version tracking. It records history but does not decide whether a change may go ahead.

options.t: Taking every change through set formal steps
options.why: Approval, ownership, impact analysis, testing, a backout plan, a window and SOPs govern a change before it reaches production.

options.t: Restarting services so a new setting applies
options.why: A restart is a technical side effect of a change, not one of the steps that govern it.

options.t: Searching the network for unpatched systems
options.why: Searching for unpatched systems is vulnerability scanning, not the process a change goes through.

explain: The business processes are the formal, repeatable steps a change passes before production, such as approval, impact analysis, test results, a backout plan and a maintenance window.

ask: Which of the following statements fits a formal change management process?

options.t: Urgent changes skip review entirely
options.why: Urgent changes take a faster path, but they are still reviewed and approved, sometimes after the fact.

options.t: Each change is first tried in production
options.why: The process gathers test results before a change reaches production, not after.

options.t: The implementer alone picks the timing
options.why: Timing comes from approval and a maintenance window, not from one implementer.

options.t: Every change has a planned way back
options.why: Every change needs a backout plan, so a failed change can be undone.

explain: A formal change process gives every change a backout plan, so a change that fails can be reversed to the last working state.

stem: An IT manager at a toy manufacturer finds that engineers change production servers whenever they have time. There is no review, no record and no plan to undo a change, and two outages followed last month.
ask: Which of the following addresses all three gaps?

options.t: Nightly backups of each server
options.why: Backups can help undo a change, but they add no review and no record.

options.t: A test lab for trying changes
options.why: A test lab adds testing, but no review, no record and no way back.

options.t: A formal change management process
options.why: A formal process adds review and approval, a recorded request and a backout plan for each change.

options.t: Letting only senior engineers make edits
options.why: Fewer people making changes still leaves no review, no record and no plan to undo.

detail: no review, no record and no plan to undo a change
explain: A formal process requires review and sign-off, a recorded request and a backout plan, so changes stop happening at random.

stem: A network engineer at a port authority asks to replace the core switch at the container terminal. A board reads her impact notes and lab test results, approves the request, and books the work for a quiet Sunday night.
ask: Which of the following does this sequence show?

options.t: A controlled change before production
options.why: Impact notes, test results, sign-off and a scheduled quiet time are the formal steps a change passes before production.

options.t: A contained security incident
options.why: Nothing has gone wrong; the switch has not even been replaced yet.

options.t: A recovery drill after a site loss
options.why: No site or system was lost. A planned replacement is being reviewed.

options.t: A scan of the network for unpatched devices
options.why: Nobody is scanning for weaknesses. A planned replacement is moving through review.

detail: approves the request, and books the work for a quiet Sunday night
explain: Reviewing impact and test results, approving, then scheduling a quiet time are the business steps that govern a change before it reaches production.

stem: The CISO of a newspaper publisher writes requirements that every production change must meet:
bullets: A named person is accountable for it
Affected departments are told in advance
A written way to undo it exists
It happens at a low-traffic time
ask: Which of the following meets all of these requirements?

options.t: Version control
options.why: Version control keeps earlier copies, but it names no accountable person and sets no schedule.

options.t: Change management
options.why: Ownership, stakeholder notice, a backout plan and a maintenance window are all parts of the change management business process.

options.t: Patch management
options.why: Patching is one kind of change. It does not by itself name owners, notify departments or plan a way back.

options.t: Incident response
options.why: Incident response handles events after they happen, not planned changes before they are made.

detail: A named person is accountable for it
explain: Each requirement is one business step of change management: ownership, stakeholders, a backout plan and a maintenance window.

stem: The IT director at a dairy cooperative wants every proposed production change reviewed by one group with members from networking, applications, security and the business. Nobody may carry out a change until that group signs off.
ask: Which of the following should the director establish?

options.t: Incident response team
options.why: An incident response team handles incidents after they occur. It does not sign off planned changes.

options.t: Audit committee
options.why: An audit committee oversees audits and their findings, not the approval of each change.

options.t: Change advisory board
options.why: A change advisory board brings members from several areas together to review and approve changes before they are made.

options.t: Security operations center
options.why: A security operations center monitors and responds to security events. It does not approve changes.

detail: Nobody may carry out a change until that group signs off
explain: Change management is usually overseen by a change advisory board (CAB), a group from several areas that reviews and approves changes before they are made.

stem: A project analyst at a shipyard sorts the items in a storage upgrade plan into two groups: the business process steps that govern the change, and the technical side effects the change may cause.
ask: Which of the following belongs with the business process steps?

options.t: Service restart
options.why: A service restart is a technical side effect of the change, not a step that governs it.

options.t: Downtime
options.why: Downtime is a technical effect the change may cause, not a governing step.

options.t: Dependencies
options.why: Dependencies are a technical implication: other systems that rely on the one being changed.

options.t: Impact analysis
options.why: Impact analysis is one of the business steps that govern a change before approval.

detail: the business process steps that govern the change
explain: The business processes are approval, ownership, stakeholders, impact analysis, test results, a backout plan, a maintenance window and SOPs. Restarts, downtime and dependencies are technical implications.

stem: An operations director at a recycling company finds that each team handles changes its own way. One team emails a manager, one posts in a group chat, and one simply makes the change. After an outage nobody can tell which path a change took.
ask: Which of the following would a change management business process give these teams?

options.t: A copy of every file version
options.why: Keeping every version is version control. It records history, but each team could still handle changes its own way.

options.t: A repeatable set of steps for every change
options.why: A business process for changes is clear and repeatable, so every team takes each change through the same steps.

options.t: A list of programs allowed to run
options.why: An allow list controls which programs run. It says nothing about how a team proposes or approves a change.

options.t: A restart of each changed service
options.why: A service restart is a technical side effect of some changes, not a set of steps every team follows.

detail: each team handles changes its own way
explain: The change management business process is clear and repeatable: every change passes the same steps, whichever team makes it.

stem: After the payroll export at an insurance brokerage stopped working, a security analyst pulls the record below from the change system.
ask: Which of the following does this record show was bypassed?

options.t: Version control
options.why: Version control could hold the old script, but the record shows missing review steps, not missing versions.

options.t: Vulnerability scanning
options.why: Scanning finds weaknesses in systems. The record shows a change made without its governing steps.

options.t: Incident response
options.why: Incident response acts after an event. The record shows how the change itself was made.

options.t: Change management
options.why: No impact analysis, no test results and no approval means the change skipped the change management process.

detail: Approval:         none recorded
explain: The script went live the same day it was requested, with no impact analysis, no test results and no approval, so the formal change process was bypassed.

stem: A new security analyst at a fishing cooperative writes a one-page summary of the change management business process for the next internal audit.
ask: Which of the following statements about the process are accurate? (Select TWO)

options.t: A change advisory board usually oversees it
options.why: Change management is usually overseen by a change advisory board that reviews and approves changes.

options.t: Only security changes go through it
options.why: Any production change can affect security, so the process covers changes of every kind, not only security ones.

options.t: Each change carries a way to undo it
options.why: Every change needs a backout plan, so a failed change can be reversed.

options.t: The owner always performs the work
options.why: The owner is accountable for a change, and the work is often done by another team.

options.t: Approval follows the work for routine changes
options.why: Routine changes are often pre-approved in advance. Approval after the work is for emergency changes.

detail: change management business process
explain: Change management is usually overseen by a change advisory board (CAB), and every change in it carries a backout plan.

ask: Which of the following describes the approval process in change management?

options.t: Naming who answers for the change
options.why: Naming who is accountable for a change is ownership, not approval.

options.t: Undoing a change that went wrong
options.why: Undoing a failed change is what a backout plan does.

options.t: Signing off the change before it is made
options.why: Approval is the formal review and sign-off of a change before anyone makes it.

options.t: Running the change on a copy in a test lab
options.why: Trying a change in a lab produces test results, which the reviewers read; it is not the sign-off.

explain: The approval process is the formal review and sign-off of a change before it is made, often by a change advisory board weighing purpose, scope, risk and schedule.

ask: Which of the following describes how the approval process treats an emergency change?

options.t: It still gets approval, sometimes afterward
options.why: Emergency changes still need approval, and that approval is sometimes given after the fact.

options.t: It needs no approval at all
options.why: An emergency change still needs approval, even when it comes after the work.

options.t: It waits for the next regular board meeting
options.why: Waiting would defeat the urgency. Approval can come after the fact instead.

options.t: Its implementer approves it alone
options.why: The person doing the work does not sign off alone; the change still goes through approval.

explain: An emergency change still needs approval. It may come after the work, but it is never simply skipped.

stem: A systems administrator at a botanical garden submits a request to open a firewall port for a ticket kiosk vendor. The request is on hold until the change advisory board meets on Thursday.
ask: What is the request waiting for?

options.t: An accountable owner to be named for it
options.why: The hold is the board meeting, and the board meets to decide on changes, not to name their owners.

options.t: Lab results from a test copy
options.why: Testing is done before the board reads a request. The hold is the board decision itself.

options.t: A quiet time slot to do the work
options.why: A time slot is booked once the change may go ahead. The request is waiting on the board decision.

options.t: Formal sign-off before work starts
options.why: A change advisory board reviews a request and signs it off before the work starts: the approval process.

detail: until the change advisory board meets
explain: The approval process reviews a request on its purpose, scope, risk and schedule and signs it off before any work starts.

stem: The marketing director at a radio station requests an upgrade to the program scheduling software and is accountable for it. A separate board of IT, security and operations members decides whether the upgrade may go ahead.
ask: What is the role of the board in this change?

options.t: Owning the change
options.why: The marketing director requested the change and is accountable for it, so the director is the owner.

options.t: Approving the change
options.why: Deciding whether a change may go ahead is the approval process, here carried out by a board.

options.t: Performing the upgrade
options.why: The stem says the board decides; nothing says it does the technical work.

options.t: Testing the upgrade
options.why: The board decides whether the change may proceed. Testing is not its job.

detail: decides whether the upgrade may go ahead
explain: The owner requests and answers for a change. A board, often a change advisory board, approves it.

stem: A database administrator at a stock exchange applies a fix at 2 a.m. to stop an active attack on the order matching system. The change advisory board cannot meet until morning.
ask: Which of the following should happen to this change under the approval process?

options.t: It is exempt from any review
options.why: An urgent change made to stop an attack still needs approval, even if it comes afterward.

options.t: It is rolled back until the board meets
options.why: Rolling back would reopen the attack. Urgent changes can be approved after the fact.

options.t: It is reviewed and approved after the fact
options.why: An emergency change still gets approval, which may come after the work is done.

options.t: It is approved by the database administrator alone
options.why: The person who made the change does not sign it off alone; the board still reviews it.

detail: to stop an active attack on the order matching system
explain: Emergency changes take a faster path: the fix goes in first and the board reviews and approves it afterward, so the change is still controlled.

stem: A network manager at a pipeline operator asks the change board to let her add a remote access gateway for field crews. The board agrees the gateway may be installed, provided the security team watches the gateway logs closely for two weeks afterward.
ask: Which of the following decisions did the board make?

options.t: Approval with conditions
options.why: The board said yes but attached a requirement, which is approval with conditions.

options.t: Deferral of the request
options.why: A deferral postpones the decision. Here the board agreed the gateway may be installed.

options.t: Rejection of the request
options.why: A rejection refuses the change. Here the board allowed it.

options.t: Emergency approval
options.why: Nothing in the stem is urgent; the request went through the normal board review.

detail: provided the security team watches the gateway logs closely for two weeks afterward
explain: A board can approve, reject, defer, or approve with conditions such as extra monitoring. Agreeing on the condition of log monitoring is a conditional approval.

stem: A quality lead at a game studio installs the new release on staging servers and records how it behaved. A separate panel then reads those records and decides whether the release may go to the live servers.
ask: Which change management step is the panel carrying out?

options.t: Test results
options.why: The quality lead produced the test results. The panel only reads them.

options.t: Impact analysis
options.why: Impact analysis predicts effects before testing. The panel is deciding whether the release may proceed.

options.t: Maintenance window
options.why: No time slot is being chosen. The panel decides whether the release may go live at all.

options.t: Approval process
options.why: Reviewing the evidence and deciding whether a change may proceed is the approval process.

detail: decides whether the release may go to the live servers
explain: Testing produces evidence; approval is the separate decision made after reviewing it. The board reviews test results but does not run the tests.

stem: An auditor at a title insurer reviews a change that enabled remote desktop on a file server. The request was logged, had lab test results and an undo plan, and was carried out during the agreed weekend hours. Nobody ever reviewed or signed it.
ask: Which step of change management was skipped?

options.t: Backout plan
options.why: The request had an undo plan, so the backout plan was in place.

options.t: Approval process
options.why: Nobody reviewed or signed the request, so the change was made without approval.

options.t: Test results
options.why: The request had lab test results, so testing was done.

options.t: Maintenance window
options.why: The work was done during the agreed weekend hours, so the window was respected.

detail: Nobody ever reviewed or signed it
explain: Every other step was present. Nobody reviewed or signed off the change, so it skipped the approval process.

stem: A change coordinator at a bus manufacturer shares the record below with the teams waiting on it.
ask: Which change management step produced the decisions in this record?

lines: CHG-8812 Add file transfer route for parts supplier
Decision: deferred, resubmit with an undo plan
CHG-8815 Replace lobby kiosk operating system

options.t: Restricted activities
options.why: Restricted activities keep implementers inside the approved scope. The record holds the board decisions themselves.

options.t: Backout plan
options.why: A missing undo plan is the reason for one deferral; the decisions themselves come from the board.

options.t: Approval process
options.why: A board deferring one change and approving another is the approval process at work.

options.t: Impact analysis
options.why: A risk rating comes from impact analysis, but deciding to defer or approve is the board sign-off.

detail: Decision: deferred, resubmit with an undo plan
explain: Change board minutes record approval decisions: approve, reject, defer, or approve with conditions. Ownership, risk ratings and undo plans are inputs the board weighs.

stem: A new change coordinator at a public library system studies how approvals work before her first change board meeting.
ask: Which of the following statements about the approval process are accurate? (Select TWO)

options.t: The board runs the tests itself
options.why: The board reviews test results that others produce; it does not run tests.

options.t: Sign-off comes before work starts
options.why: A normal change is reviewed and signed off before the work starts.

options.t: Approval replaces the impact analysis
options.why: The board reads the impact analysis as an input; approval does not replace it.

options.t: Urgent changes may be approved afterward
options.why: Emergency changes still get approval, sometimes after the fact.

options.t: Routine changes are never recorded
options.why: Routine changes are still recorded; low-risk ones may be pre-approved, which is itself approval.

detail: studies how approvals work
explain: Approval is a sign-off before work starts. An emergency change can be approved after the fact, but it is still approved and recorded.

ask: Which of the following describes the owner of a change?

options.t: The party accountable for the change
options.why: The owner requests the change and is accountable for it and the affected system.

options.t: Everyone whose work the change affects
options.why: The people a change affects are its stakeholders, a wider group than the owner.

options.t: The group that signs off on the change
options.why: Signing off is the approval process, usually a change advisory board.

options.t: Whoever performs the technical work
options.why: The owner is often not the one doing the work; another team may carry it out.

explain: The owner is the person or group responsible for a change and the system it affects. The owner is accountable even when someone else does the work.

ask: Which of the following statements about change ownership is accurate?

options.t: The owner always does the technical work
options.why: The owner is not always the implementer; IT or a contractor often does the work.

options.t: The owner is kept informed of the change
options.why: The owner is accountable for the change and is kept informed as it goes.

options.t: The owner is whoever signs the approval
options.why: Sign-off is the approval process. The owner requests and answers for the change.

options.t: Ownership passes to IT once work begins
options.why: The owner stays accountable for the whole change, even while IT does the work.

explain: The owner stays accountable for the change from request to finish and is kept informed, whoever does the technical work.

stem: The head of the call center at a power utility asks IT to upgrade the call recording software. IT will install it, but the head of the call center alone answers for the result.
ask: Which of the following does this arrangement show?

options.t: A change made with no one accountable
options.why: Someone is accountable: the stem says the call center head answers for the result.

options.t: Accountability shared by the two teams
options.why: The stem says the call center head alone answers for the result.

options.t: An implementer who answers for the result
options.why: IT does the installing, but it is not the one that answers for the result.

options.t: An owner who does not do the work
options.why: The call center head requested the change and answers for it, while IT does the work.

detail: the head of the call center alone answers for the result
explain: The owner requests and is accountable for a change but does not have to perform it. Here IT installs and the call center head owns.

stem: At a home health agency, the scheduling app belongs to the nursing manager, who asked for its update. A contractor from an outside firm will install the update next week after a review board signs off.
ask: Which of the following is accountable for this change?

options.t: The contractor installing it
options.why: The contractor only performs the work. Doing the work does not make someone accountable for the change.

options.t: The board that signs it off
options.why: The board approves the change. Approval is a separate role from ownership.

options.t: The business owner of the app
options.why: The nursing manager owns the app and requested the update, so the manager is accountable.

options.t: The staff who book patient visits
options.why: Staff who use the app are affected by the change, but they did not request it and do not answer for it.

detail: the scheduling app belongs to the nursing manager, who asked for its update
explain: The owner of the system requests the change and answers for it. The contractor implements and the board approves, but neither is the owner.

stem: The finance director at a cruise line asks IT to replace the expense reporting system. Her department uses the system every day, and she answers to the executive team for the outcome of the replacement.
ask: Which of the following BEST describes the role of the finance director in this change?

options.t: Approval process
options.why: Nothing says she signs off the change. She requested it and answers for its outcome.

options.t: Ownership
options.why: She requested the change and is accountable for its outcome, which makes her the owner.

options.t: Stakeholders
options.why: Her department is affected, so she is also a stakeholder, but she is accountable for the outcome too, which is ownership.

options.t: Impact analysis
options.why: Impact analysis is an assessment of risks, not a role a person holds.

detail: she answers to the executive team for the outcome of the replacement
edge: A stakeholder is anyone the change affects. Being accountable for the outcome is what makes her the owner.
explain: Her department is affected, but she also requested the change and answers for its result. Accountability is the mark of the owner.

stem: After a failed upgrade of the ticketing software at a symphony orchestra, the general manager finds every department blaming another. Nobody can say who requested the change or who answers for its result.
ask: Which part of the change management business process was missing?

options.t: Ownership
options.why: Nobody knowing who requested the change or who answers for it means no owner was assigned.

options.t: Stakeholders
options.why: Several departments were clearly affected. The gap is that none of them was accountable.

options.t: Backout plan
options.why: Undoing the upgrade would not tell anyone who answers for it.

options.t: Maintenance window
options.why: A scheduled time says when the work happens, not who answers for it.

detail: Nobody can say who requested the change or who answers for its result
explain: Ownership makes responsibility clear: one named person or group requests the change and is accountable for it. Without it a failure belongs to nobody.

stem: Midway through a database migration at a tax preparation firm, the IT team hits an error that will push the finish past Monday morning. The client services director requested the migration and is accountable for it.
ask: Which of the following should happen under change management ownership?

options.t: IT decides alone and reports later
options.why: The owner is accountable and kept informed, so IT does not keep the delay to itself.

options.t: The work goes on without any notice
options.why: A delay affects the owner, who must be kept informed.

options.t: Ownership moves to the IT team
options.why: Ownership does not move to whoever is doing the work when problems arise.

options.t: The owner is told about the delay
options.why: The owner is accountable for the change and is kept informed, including about delays.

detail: requested the migration and is accountable for it
explain: The director owns the change, and an owner is kept informed throughout. A delay that pushes the finish past Monday is exactly what the owner must hear about.

stem: An auditor at a food bank asks who is responsible for the donor database and its future upgrades. She does not want to know who carried out the last upgrade, only who answers for the system and its changes.
ask: Which part of change management answers the question of the auditor?

options.t: Version control
options.why: Version control shows who made each past edit, which the auditor says she does not need.

options.t: Stakeholders
options.why: Stakeholders are everyone affected, not the one party that answers for the system.

options.t: Ownership
options.why: Ownership names who is responsible for the system and accountable for its changes.

options.t: Approval process
options.why: Approval signs off each change. It does not name who answers for the system.

detail: only who answers for the system and its changes
explain: Ownership assigns the person or group responsible for a change and for the affected system, so it tells the auditor who answers for the database.

stem: A help desk analyst at a grocery wholesaler reads the change record below while the ticket waits to be closed.
ask: Who should confirm that the upgraded printers meet the business need before CHG-3307 is closed?

options.t: The person who asked for the change
options.why: Okafor requested the change and is accountable for it as its owner, so the owner confirms the result is acceptable.

options.t: The technician who installed it
options.why: Desktop Support performed the work. Doing the work does not make it the party that answers for the business need.

options.t: The change board
options.why: The board decided whether the change could go ahead. Confirming that the result serves the business is the owner's part.

options.t: The help desk analyst
options.why: The analyst only reads the record. Nothing makes the help desk accountable for this change.

detail: Close needs:   result confirmed by ____
explain: The owner requests a change and answers for its outcome, so the owner confirms the result is acceptable before the change is closed, even when IT did the work.

stem: A department head at a dental supply distributor has just been named owner of a planned upgrade to the order entry system. IT will carry out the upgrade.
ask: Which of the following are responsibilities of the department head as owner? (Select TWO)

options.t: Answer for the outcome of the change
options.why: The owner is accountable for the change and its result.

options.t: Perform the installation work
options.why: IT will carry out the upgrade; the owner does not have to do the technical work.

options.t: Sign off as the change board
options.why: Approval comes from the approval process, not from the owner acting as the board.

options.t: Stay informed as the work proceeds
options.why: The owner is kept informed throughout the change.

options.t: Run the tests in the staging lab
options.why: Testing produces evidence for approval; it is not an ownership duty.

detail: IT will carry out the upgrade
explain: An owner is accountable for the change and kept informed, while others may do the work, test it and approve it.

ask: Which of the following does the stakeholders step of change management require?

options.t: Naming the one person accountable
options.why: Naming who is accountable is ownership, not the stakeholders step.

options.t: Identifying and consulting everyone affected
options.why: Stakeholders are the people and groups a change affects, and they are identified and consulted.

options.t: Rating the risk as high, medium or low
options.why: Rating the risk of a change is part of impact analysis.

options.t: Trying the change in a test environment
options.why: Trying a change outside production produces test results.

explain: Stakeholders are everyone a change may affect. They are identified and consulted because the change may impact their work.

ask: Which of the following statements about stakeholders in change management is accurate?

options.t: Only the owner counts as a stakeholder
options.why: Stakeholders are anyone the change impacts, a much wider group than the owner.

options.t: They are told only after the change
options.why: Stakeholders are involved in planning and communication, before the change too.

options.t: Even small changes can affect many departments
options.why: Even a small change can reach many departments, so all of them are stakeholders.

options.t: They must all hold technical roles
options.why: Anyone impacted is a stakeholder, whatever their job.

explain: A change that looks small to IT can reach many departments. Everyone impacted is a stakeholder and is involved in planning and communication.

stem: An IT analyst at a regional rail operator plans to update the fare database. Before scheduling it, she lists the ticket offices, the finance team, the mobile app vendor and the help desk, and asks each how the update could affect their work.
ask: Which change management step is she carrying out?

options.t: Stakeholders
options.why: Listing everyone the change affects and consulting them is the stakeholders step.

options.t: Ownership
options.why: Ownership names who is accountable. She is listing and consulting everyone affected.

options.t: Approval process
options.why: Nobody is signing off the change; she is asking affected groups about their work.

options.t: Test results
options.why: Nothing has been tried yet. She is consulting the groups the update affects.

detail: asks each how the update could affect their work
explain: Identifying the people and groups a change affects and consulting them in planning is the stakeholders step.

stem: An application developer at a candle maker updated the order system overnight. The update had been analyzed for impact, tested and approved, and it worked as planned. It also moved the label reprint button on the screen the packing team uses, and nobody had asked that team about the new layout.
ask: Which part of the change management process was overlooked?

options.t: Impact analysis
options.why: The stem says the update was analyzed for impact.

options.t: Test results
options.why: The stem says the update was tested and worked as planned.

options.t: Approval process
options.why: The stem says the update was approved.

options.t: Stakeholders
options.why: The packing team was affected by the new layout but was never consulted, so the stakeholders were not involved.

detail: nobody had asked that team about the new layout
explain: Every other step was done. The packing team works on the changed screen, so it was a stakeholder that should have been consulted before the change.

stem: The data engineering manager at a sporting goods retailer requested a new layout for the shared customer database. Sales, finance and an outside marketing agency all build their weekly reports from that database.
ask: Which of the following BEST describes sales, finance and the agency in this change?

options.t: Ownership
options.why: The data engineering manager requested the change. The other groups did not and do not answer for it.

options.t: Approval process
options.why: Nothing says these groups sign off the change. Their work is affected by it.

options.t: Stakeholders
options.why: Sales, finance and the agency are groups whose work the change affects, which makes them stakeholders.

options.t: Dependencies
options.why: Their reports rely on the database, but dependencies describe components that rely on each other, not affected groups.

detail: all build their weekly reports from that database
edge: Dependencies are relationships between components. The question asks about the groups whose work is affected, which is stakeholders.
explain: Groups whose work a change affects are its stakeholders, whether inside the company or outside it like the agency.

stem: Before moving the scanners at a frozen food distributor to a new wireless network, the network lead meets the night shift supervisors who use them. They warn that the freezer aisles already have weak signal.
ask: Which change management practice brought this warning to light?

options.t: Test results
options.why: Nothing has been tried yet. The warning came from a conversation.

options.t: Stakeholders
options.why: Consulting the people who use the scanners, as stakeholders, surfaced a risk the network lead did not know.

options.t: Approval process
options.why: No sign-off is involved. The warning came from consulting users.

options.t: Version control
options.why: Version control tracks file history. It played no part in the warning.

detail: meets the night shift supervisors who use them
explain: Stakeholders are involved in planning because they often know risks the implementers do not, such as weak signal in the freezer aisles.

stem: The day before a planned outage of the email system at a law school, the IT manager sends a notice to faculty, students and the admissions office. It gives the outage time and explains the new sign-in screen they will see afterward.
ask: Which part of the change management business process does the notice BEST serve?

options.t: Stakeholders
options.why: Telling everyone affected what will happen and how things will change is stakeholder communication.

options.t: Maintenance window
options.why: The notice mentions the outage time, but the window is the time itself; the notice informs the people affected.

options.t: Approval process
options.why: The notice informs affected groups. It is not a sign-off.

options.t: Test results
options.why: The notice reports no evidence from trying the change; it tells affected groups what will happen.

detail: sends a notice to faculty, students and the admissions office
edge: The maintenance window is when the outage happens. A notice to the affected groups about it, and about the new screen, serves the stakeholders.
explain: Faculty, students and admissions are stakeholders. Telling them about the outage and the new sign-in screen is the communication that stakeholders need.

stem: A mail administrator at a tile manufacturer plans to change the sender address used on all outgoing company email and calls it a five-minute job. Billing sends invoices from it, marketing's newsletter tool checks it, and the support desk sorts customer replies by it.
ask: Which of the following should the administrator do before making the change?

options.t: Make it and watch for complaints
options.why: Waiting for complaints means the affected groups learn of the change only when it breaks their work.

options.t: Ask only his own team to review it
options.why: His own team is not the only group affected; billing, marketing and support are too.

options.t: Skip review because it is small
options.why: A small change can still affect many departments, as this one does.

options.t: Consult the groups that rely on it
options.why: Billing, marketing and support all rely on the address, so they are stakeholders to involve.

detail: Billing sends invoices from it, marketing's newsletter tool checks it, and the support desk sorts customer replies by it
explain: A change that looks small can reach many departments. Everyone it affects is a stakeholder to consult before the change.

stem: After a change at a commercial real estate firm, a security analyst reviews the change record below.
ask: Which of the following does the outcome line show went wrong?

lines: CHG-6610 Retire old file share fs02
Outcome: Legal lost access to its lease archive on fs02

options.t: The change was never signed off
options.why: The record shows the change board approved it on 05/03.

options.t: The list left out an affected group
options.why: Legal relied on fs02 but is missing from the stakeholder list, so it was never consulted.

options.t: The change was never tested
options.why: The record shows it was tested in staging on 05/01.

options.t: The owner did the work alone
options.why: The record says nothing about who did the work; the problem is who was left off the list.

detail: Outcome: Legal lost access to its lease archive on fs02
explain: Legal used the share but was not on the stakeholder list. Missing a stakeholder causes exactly this kind of surprise outage.

stem: A project coordinator at an eyewear retail chain writes guidance on working with the store staff and customers affected by a coming replacement of the appointment booking system.
ask: Which of the following practices match how stakeholders are handled in change management? (Select TWO)

options.t: Consult them while planning the change
options.why: Stakeholders are involved in planning, because the change may impact their work.

options.t: Tell them only if the change fails
options.why: Stakeholders are kept informed whether or not anything goes wrong.

options.t: Limit them to the IT department
options.why: Stakeholders are anyone impacted, here store staff and customers outside IT.

options.t: Tell them before service is interrupted
options.why: Communication with stakeholders includes warning them before an interruption.

options.t: Let them sign off in place of the board
options.why: Being affected does not make a group the approver; approval stays with the approval process.

detail: working with the store staff and customers affected
explain: Stakeholders are involved in planning and communication: they are consulted early and told about interruptions before they happen.

ask: Which of the following describes impact analysis for a change?

options.t: Confirming the change works in a test lab
options.why: Confirming a change works in a lab produces test results. Impact analysis predicts.

options.t: Signing off the change before it is made
options.why: Signing off is the approval process, which reads the impact analysis.

options.t: Naming who answers for the change
options.why: Naming who is accountable is ownership.

options.t: Assessing risks of changing and of not changing
options.why: Impact analysis weighs the risks of making the change and of leaving things as they are.

explain: Impact analysis assesses the risks of making a change and of not making it, including failures, side effects and the effect on business operations.

source.chapter: Impact analysis (change impact and security impact analysis)

ask: Which of the following pairs of questions does an impact analysis answer?

options.t: What could break, and what if we wait?
options.why: Impact analysis covers both the risk of the change and the risk of doing nothing.

options.t: Who answers for it, and who must be told?
options.why: Those questions belong to ownership and to stakeholders.

options.t: Did it run in the lab, and did it pass?
options.why: Those questions are answered by test results.

options.t: Who signs it, and on which date?
options.why: Those questions belong to the approval process.

explain: An impact analysis asks what the change could affect and what risk remains if the change is not made.

source.chapter: Impact analysis (change impact and security impact analysis)

stem: A security engineer at a concert ticketing agency wants a stricter password rule on the customer sign-in service. Before the board meets, she writes down that older mobile apps may fail to sign in, and that leaving the rule as it is keeps accounts open to guessing attacks.
ask: Which change management step has she completed?

options.t: Test results
options.why: Nothing has been tried yet; she is predicting what could happen.

options.t: Approval process
options.why: The board has not met, so nothing has been signed off.

options.t: Impact analysis
options.why: Listing possible failures and the risk of not changing is impact analysis.

options.t: Stakeholders
options.why: She has not consulted any affected group; she has assessed risks.

detail: leaving the rule as it is keeps accounts open to guessing attacks
explain: She predicted a side effect of the change and the risk of doing nothing, before approval. That is impact analysis.

source.chapter: Impact analysis (change impact and security impact analysis)

stem: A systems administrator at a vending machine operator reviews a proposed patch for the payment terminals before the change board meets. He notes that installing it would take card payments offline for two hours, and that the planned date is the busiest sales day of the month. He rates the change medium risk.
ask: Which of the following is he assessing?

options.t: The owner accountable for the terminals
options.why: He is rating what the patch could do, not naming who answers for the terminals.

options.t: The groups to tell about the patch
options.why: He is not deciding who to tell; he is rating what the patch could do to sales.

options.t: The lab results for the patch
options.why: Nothing has been tried in a lab. He is assessing the patch in advance.

options.t: The effects the patch could have
options.why: Weighing what the patch would do to business operations and rating the risk is impact analysis.

detail: would take card payments offline for two hours
explain: Impact analysis looks at what a change could do to business operations, such as payments going offline on a busy day, and rates the risk before approval.

source.chapter: Impact analysis (change impact and security impact analysis)

stem: Before upgrading the content system at a magazine publisher, a web engineer reads the release notes and lists every plug-in and integration that the upgrade could break. Nothing has been installed anywhere yet.
ask: Which of the following BEST describes the work of the engineer?

options.t: Test results
options.why: Nothing has been installed anywhere, so there are no test results.

options.t: Dependencies
options.why: The plug-ins and integrations are dependencies, but the engineer is assessing what could break, which is the analysis.

options.t: Impact analysis
options.why: Predicting what the upgrade could break before anything is installed is impact analysis.

options.t: Business impact analysis
options.why: A business impact analysis measures the effect of losing a business function for continuity planning, not one upgrade.

detail: lists every plug-in and integration that the upgrade could break
edge: Dependencies are the relationships between components. Assessing which of them the upgrade could break, before approval, is impact analysis.
explain: Impact analysis identifies side effects before a change is approved. Mapping what an upgrade could break is part of it.

source.chapter: Impact analysis (change impact and security impact analysis)

stem: At a frozen yogurt chain, the continuity manager measures how long the order desk can stay down before losses grow. Separately, an IT analyst works out what a firmware update on the order servers could break and what happens if it is skipped.
ask: Which of the following is the IT analyst performing?

options.t: Impact analysis
options.why: Working out what one change could break and the risk of skipping it is impact analysis.

options.t: Business impact analysis
options.why: That is the continuity manager measuring the cost of the order desk being down, not the analyst.

options.t: Test results
options.why: The analyst is predicting effects, not running the update in a test environment.

options.t: Disaster recovery
options.why: Nothing has failed; the analyst is assessing a planned update.

detail: works out what a firmware update on the order servers could break
explain: Impact analysis looks at one change. A business impact analysis belongs to continuity planning and measures the effect of losing a business function.

source.chapter: Impact analysis (change impact and security impact analysis)

stem: A team lead at a medical courier service wants to delay a TLS library update until after the busy season. A security analyst objects, pointing out that attackers are already using the flaw in the current version.
ask: Which part of an impact analysis is the analyst stressing?

options.t: The risk the update itself carries
options.why: The analyst is not talking about what the update could break.

options.t: The results of a lab trial
options.why: No lab trial is mentioned; the analyst is arguing about risk.

options.t: The owner of the courier systems
options.why: The objection is about risk, not about who is accountable.

options.t: The risk of not making the change
options.why: A flaw attackers already use is the risk of leaving things unchanged.

detail: attackers are already using the flaw in the current version
explain: Impact analysis covers the risk of doing nothing as well as the risk of the change. An actively exploited flaw makes waiting risky.

source.chapter: Impact analysis (change impact and security impact analysis)

stem: After a database update at a crop insurance firm broke the claims export, a reviewer finds that the update had passed lab tests that did not cover the export, was approved and ran in the agreed window. Nobody had asked beforehand what the update might affect.
ask: Which step was skipped?

options.t: Test results
options.why: The update did pass lab tests; their gap came from nobody predicting the export could be affected.

options.t: Impact analysis
options.why: Nobody asked what the update might affect, so the side effect on the export was never identified.

options.t: Approval process
options.why: The stem says the update was approved.

options.t: Maintenance window
options.why: The stem says it ran in the agreed window.

detail: Nobody had asked beforehand what the update might affect
explain: Impact analysis identifies side effects before approval. Without it, the tests never covered the export, because no one knew it was at risk.

source.chapter: Impact analysis (change impact and security impact analysis)

stem: A change board member at a hospice network reads the impact section below and sends it back to the network engineer before the vote.
ask: Which part of an impact analysis is missing from this section?

lines: CHG-7702 Upgrade VPN gateway firmware 9.1 to 9.4
Affects: 2 gateways, 640 remote staff, MFA plug-in v3
Risk if done: MFA plug-in may fail to load (medium)
Overall rating: medium; extra plug-in testing advised

options.t: The systems the upgrade affects
options.why: The Affects line lists the gateways, the remote staff and the plug-in.

options.t: The risk of not making the change
options.why: Impact analysis rates the risk of doing nothing too. The section rates only the risk of upgrading.

options.t: A rating of the overall risk
options.why: The section gives an overall rating of medium.

options.t: The side effects of upgrading
options.why: The Risk if done line names a side effect: the plug-in may fail to load.

detail: Risk if done: MFA plug-in may fail to load (medium)
explain: An impact analysis weighs the risk of making a change and the risk of not making it. Without the second, the board cannot see what staying on the old firmware costs.

source.chapter: Impact analysis (change impact and security impact analysis)

stem: A security analyst at a car parts maker drafts the impact analysis for switching off an old file sharing protocol on every server.
ask: Which of the following belong in the analysis? (Select TWO)

options.t: The board decision on the request
options.why: The board decides after reading the analysis; its decision is not part of it.

options.t: Systems that may stop working
options.why: Possible failures and side effects are part of impact analysis.

options.t: Lab results from a trial run
options.why: Results from trying the change are test results, a separate step.

options.t: The risk if the protocol stays on
options.why: Impact analysis also covers the risk of not making the change.

options.t: The steps to undo the change
options.why: Undo steps form the backout plan, a separate part of the request.

detail: drafts the impact analysis
explain: Impact analysis covers what the change could break and what risk remains if the change is not made.

source.chapter: Impact analysis (change impact and security impact analysis)

ask: Which of the following describes test results in change management?

options.t: A forecast of what the change could break
options.why: A forecast made before anything runs is impact analysis.

options.t: Sign-off from the change review board
options.why: Sign-off is the approval process, which reads the test results.

options.t: Evidence from trying the change outside production
options.why: Test results come from trying the change in a sandbox or test lab before production.

options.t: A list of groups the change will affect
options.why: A list of affected groups is the stakeholders step.

explain: Test results are evidence from trying a change in a non-production environment, showing it works and has no harmful side effects before approval or rollout.

ask: Which of the following statements about test results is accurate?

options.t: They support the approval decision
options.why: Test results are evidence the approvers use when deciding on a change.

options.t: They come from the production system
options.why: Testing happens in a sandbox or staging environment, not in production.

options.t: They remove the need for approval
options.why: Results support approval; the change still needs it.

options.t: They predict effects without running anything
options.why: Predicting effects without running anything is impact analysis.

explain: Test results come from a non-production environment and give the approvers evidence that the change works.

stem: Before rolling a new antivirus engine out to 2,000 checkout terminals, an endpoint engineer at a home improvement chain installs it on six spare terminals in the lab. She confirms that sales still complete and receipts still print.
ask: Which change management step is the engineer carrying out?

options.t: Impact analysis
options.why: The engine was actually installed and observed, not just assessed on paper.

options.t: Test results
options.why: Trying the change on lab terminals and confirming it works produces test results.

options.t: Approval process
options.why: Nobody is signing off; the engineer is gathering evidence.

options.t: Stakeholders
options.why: She is not consulting affected groups; she is trying the change.

detail: installs it on six spare terminals in the lab
explain: Applying the change in a lab and checking that it works, before production, is how test results are gathered.

stem: A web developer at a bicycle retailer has approval for a new checkout setting, and the store manager who owns the site has told all staff about it. To save a day, the developer plans to try the setting first on the live store instead of a test copy.
ask: Which of the following is wrong with this plan?

options.t: It skips the approval process
options.why: The stem says the developer has approval.

options.t: It leaves the change without an owner
options.why: The store manager owns the site.

options.t: It leaves the staff uninformed
options.why: The owner has already told all staff.

options.t: It tests the change in production
options.why: Changes are tested in a sandbox or test copy, not on the live store.

detail: try the setting first on the live store instead of a test copy
explain: Test results should come from a sandbox or staging copy, not production, so problems are found before customers meet them.

stem: Before a change board meeting at a crane rental company, a database engineer attaches test results for a database patch. The results came from a cloned server running patch build 7.2.1, while the change request plans to install build 7.2.4 in production.
ask: Which of the following is wrong with these test results?

options.t: They tested a different change than planned
options.why: Testing proves something only when the change is applied exactly as planned. Build 7.2.1 says little about build 7.2.4.

options.t: They came from outside production
options.why: Testing outside production is the point: the clone is where the change should be tried first.

options.t: They were gathered before approval
options.why: Test results are meant to be gathered before approval, so the board can use them.

options.t: They omit the risk of not making the change
options.why: The risk of doing nothing belongs in the impact analysis, not in the test results.

detail: while the change request plans to install build 7.2.4 in production
explain: Test results count only when the change is applied exactly as planned for production. Results from another build prove nothing about the build that will be installed.

stem: A quality engineer at a lottery operator tests a new draw results feed on a staging server that runs an older database version than production. Every test passes, but the feed fails on its first night in production.
ask: Which of the following explains why the test results were misleading?

options.t: The tests ran on the production server
options.why: The stem says the tests ran on a staging server.

options.t: The staging server skipped some tests
options.why: The stem says every test passed, so none were skipped.

options.t: The staging setup did not match production
options.why: A test environment with an older database version than production can pass changes that fail live.

options.t: The board approved it with no testing
options.why: The feed was tested before it went live; every test passed.

detail: runs an older database version than production
explain: Test results are only as good as the environment. A staging server that does not match production gives false confidence.

stem: An engineer at a seafood exporter installs new firmware on the lab copies of the warehouse routers. Then she reverts one lab router to the old firmware and confirms it works as it did before.
ask: Which of the following is the purpose of the second step?

options.t: To measure the risk of not upgrading
options.why: Weighing the risk of not upgrading is impact analysis, done on paper.

options.t: To check that a rollback succeeds
options.why: Testing also covers the backout plan, so the team knows it can return to the old firmware.

options.t: To approve the firmware for production
options.why: Approval is a sign-off by reviewers, not a lab step.

options.t: To tell the warehouse about the change
options.why: Reverting a lab router informs nobody; it checks the way back.

detail: reverts one lab router to the old firmware
explain: Testing a change includes testing its backout, so the team knows the way back works before it is ever needed.

stem: A network engineer at an online plant nursery runs a planned load balancer change on the staging pair before the change board meets. Traffic is balanced correctly, but the balancer's admin page now opens without asking for a password.
ask: Which of the following do these test results show?

options.t: The change weakens a security control
options.why: Testing checks security as well as function. An admin page that no longer asks for a password is a harmful side effect.

options.t: The change is ready for production
options.why: It works for traffic, but it has a harmful side effect, so it is not ready.

options.t: The staging pair differs from production
options.why: Nothing in the stem says the staging pair differs from production.

options.t: The backout plan has been tested
options.why: Nobody undid the change in staging, so the backout was not tested.

detail: the balancer's admin page now opens without asking for a password
explain: Test results confirm a change works and has no harmful side effects. This one works but drops a password check, so it should not be approved as it is.

stem: A change board member at a museum ticketing service reads the test log below before the weekly meeting.
ask: Which of the following should the board do based on this log?

lines: Staging run 04/09  CHG-2214 kiosk OS update
Revert to old image  OK in 9 min

options.t: Approve the update for all kiosks
options.why: A failure is still open in staging, so the evidence does not support approval.

options.t: Approve it and skip the backout plan
options.why: The revert worked in staging, which is a reason to keep the backout plan, not drop it.

options.t: Hold approval until printing passes
options.why: The results show a failed side effect, so the change should not be approved until it passes.

options.t: Try the update on live kiosks first
options.why: Testing belongs outside production; trying it live would bring the failure to customers.

detail: Receipt print ..... FAIL (3/12)
explain: Test results support the approval decision. A failure found in staging means the change is not ready, even though other checks and the revert passed.

stem: A systems engineer at a construction firm writes the test plan for an upgrade of the employee self-service portal.
ask: Which of the following should the tests confirm? (Select TWO)

options.t: Staff can still sign in and work
options.why: Tests confirm the change works as intended for the people who use it.

options.t: The board has signed the request
options.why: Sign-off is the approval process, which comes from reviewers, not tests.

options.t: Security settings stayed in place
options.why: Tests check for harmful side effects, such as a security setting reset by the upgrade.

options.t: An owner has been named
options.why: Naming an owner is ownership; no test confirms it.

options.t: The live portal was used for tests
options.why: Tests run in a sandbox or staging copy, not on the live portal.

detail: writes the test plan for an upgrade
explain: Testing confirms a change works and has no harmful side effects, including on security settings, before it reaches production.

ask: Which of the following describes a backout plan?

options.t: A scheduled quiet time for changes
options.why: A scheduled quiet time for changes is a maintenance window.

options.t: A documented way to undo a failed change
options.why: A backout plan returns a system to its previous working state if a change fails.

options.t: Written steps for a routine task
options.why: Written steps for routine work are a standard operating procedure.

options.t: An assessment of what a change could break
options.why: Assessing what a change could break is impact analysis.

explain: A backout plan is a documented way to undo a change and return to the previous working state if the change fails or causes problems.

ask: Which of the following statements about backout plans is accurate?

options.t: Only large changes need one
options.why: A backout plan is always required, whatever the size of the change.

options.t: It is written after a change fails
options.why: The plan is prepared before the change, so it is ready if the change fails.

options.t: Backups make it unnecessary
options.why: A backout plan usually depends on good backups; backups do not replace it.

options.t: It usually depends on good backups
options.why: A backout plan usually relies on backups or snapshots of the earlier state.

explain: A backout plan is always required and usually relies on good backups or snapshots of the earlier state. The backups alone are not the plan.

stem: Before switching the core router at a trucking firm to a new routing setup, a network engineer exports the current configuration. He also writes the exact commands to load it again if traffic stops flowing after the switch.
ask: Which change management element is the engineer preparing?

options.t: Backout plan
options.why: Saving the current state and writing how to restore it is a backout plan.

options.t: Maintenance window
options.why: Nothing in the stem chooses a time for the work.

options.t: Test results
options.why: Nothing has been tried yet; he is preparing a way back.

options.t: Impact analysis
options.why: He is not rating risks; he is preparing to restore the old setup.

detail: writes the exact commands to load it again if traffic stops flowing
explain: A backout plan captures the current working state and documents how to return to it if the change fails.

stem: The IT lead at a plumbing supply wholesaler is about to start tonight's upgrade of the billing system. The work is approved, tested and scheduled, but she refuses to begin until someone writes down how to return to the current version if the upgrade fails.
ask: Which change management element is the IT lead asking for?

options.t: Stakeholders
options.why: She is not asking who is affected; she wants a written way back to the current version.

options.t: Impact analysis
options.why: Impact analysis rates the risk of a change. She wants a way back if the upgrade fails.

options.t: Backout plan
options.why: Writing down how to return to the current version if the change fails is the backout plan.

options.t: Test results
options.why: The stem says the work is already tested. She wants a way back, not more evidence.

detail: how to return to the current version if the upgrade fails
explain: A backout plan is a documented way to return to the previous working state, and it is prepared before the change starts, not after it fails.

stem: Halfway through a change to the order database at a furniture retailer, the migration script fails. No hardware or site was lost. The team restores the snapshot taken just before the change, and the store is back online in fifteen minutes.
ask: Which of the following BEST describes what the team carried out?

options.t: Test results
options.why: This happened in production during the real change, not in a test environment.

options.t: Disaster recovery
options.why: Service was restored after a failure, but disaster recovery covers losing a whole site or system, and nothing like that was lost.

options.t: Maintenance window
options.why: A window is the time the work happens, not the act of undoing it.

options.t: Backout plan
options.why: Returning to the state from just before one failed change is the backout plan at work.

detail: No hardware or site was lost
edge: Both restore service, but disaster recovery handles losing a site or system. Undoing one failed change, with nothing lost, is a backout.
explain: A backout plan undoes one change that failed. Disaster recovery is for losing a whole site or system from any cause, which did not happen here.

stem: A storage administrator at a radiology group argues that a planned change to the imaging archive needs no backout plan, because the archive is backed up every night.
ask: Which of the following explains why the nightly backups alone are not enough?

options.t: Backups are never used for undo
options.why: A backout plan usually relies on good backups, so they are used.

options.t: Backups lack the documented undo steps
options.why: A backup is a tool. The backout plan documents how to use it to get back to the working state.

options.t: A backout plan replaces all backups
options.why: The plan depends on backups; it does not replace them.

options.t: Backups only serve disaster recovery
options.why: Backups also support backing out a single change.

detail: because the archive is backed up every night
explain: A backout plan is a documented way back and is always required. It usually depends on backups, but having backups is not the same as having the plan.

stem: The vendor of the card readers at a parking garage operator states that its new firmware cannot be downgraded once installed. An engineer asks what this means for the change request.
ask: Which of the following is true of the backout plan for this update?

options.t: It is still required before approval
options.why: Every change needs a backout plan, and a hard-to-reverse change needs one most.

options.t: It can be skipped, since undo is impossible
options.why: A backout plan is always required; it may need another way back, such as spare readers on the old firmware.

options.t: It can be written after the update fails
options.why: The plan is prepared before the change so it is ready when needed.

options.t: It can be replaced by the release notes
options.why: Release notes describe the update; they are not a documented way back.

detail: cannot be downgraded once installed
explain: Not every change is easy to reverse. That makes the backout plan more important, not optional, and it must be ready before the change is approved.

stem: A database administrator at a ski equipment rental chain books an upgrade into a four-hour overnight window. Lab testing shows the upgrade takes three hours, and restoring the old version takes two.
ask: Which of the following problems does this reveal?

options.t: The upgrade is too slow to test
options.why: It was tested in the lab; the timing came from that test.

options.t: The window is longer than needed
options.why: Three hours of upgrade plus two of restore is more than four, so the window is too short.

options.t: The window has no room for a late backout
options.why: If the upgrade fails near its end, the two-hour restore would run past the window.

options.t: The restore removes the need for approval
options.why: A way back never replaces approval.

detail: restoring the old version takes two
explain: A backout plan has to fit inside the window. Three hours of upgrade and two of restore cannot both fit in four, so a late failure would overrun.

stem: An engineer at a corporate campus security office watches the log below during a badge server change.
ask: What should the team do NEXT?

lines: Plan trigger: door controllers offline over 10 min after cutover
02:00 cutover to new badge server complete

options.t: Wait for the next maintenance window
options.why: The trigger was already met at 02:15. Waiting leaves the doors without working controllers.

options.t: Follow the steps to revert the change
options.why: The controllers have been offline over 10 minutes, so the planned trigger for backing out is met.

options.t: Keep the new server and fix it live

detail: 02:15 door controllers offline: 6

stem: A systems engineer at a regional television station prepares the backout plan for a firmware upgrade of the broadcast storage array.
ask: Which of the following belong in the backout plan? (Select TWO)

options.t: A list of departments to notify
options.why: Departments to notify are stakeholders, a separate part of the request.

options.t: Steps to return to the old firmware
options.why: The plan documents how to undo the change.

options.t: A rating of the risk of the change
options.why: Rating risk is impact analysis.

options.t: A saved copy of the current settings
options.why: Capturing the current state lets the team return to it, which the plan depends on.

options.t: The approved time slot for the work
options.why: The time slot is the maintenance window.

detail: prepares the backout plan
explain: A backout plan holds what is needed to return to the previous working state: the saved current state and the steps to restore it.

ask: Which question about a change does a maintenance window answer?

options.t: Whether it may be made

options.t: How it can be undone

options.t: When it may be made
options.why: A maintenance window is the scheduled time set aside for making changes.

options.t: Who answers for it
options.why: Who is accountable for a change is ownership.

explain: A maintenance window is about when: a scheduled period, usually of low business activity, set aside for changes so disruption is minimized.

ask: Which of the following describes a change freeze?

options.t: A pause on changes during a critical period
options.why: A freeze blocks routine changes during critical business periods, such as a peak season.

options.t: A copy of a system saved before a change
options.why: A saved copy supports a backout plan; it does not stop changes.

options.t: A rejection of one request by the board
options.why: A board rejecting one request is the approval process, not a period with no changes.

stem: The IT manager at a fitness club chain books all server updates for Sunday from 3 a.m. to 5 a.m. The clubs are closed then and the booking site has almost no visitors.

options.why: Nothing here describes how to undo an update; it sets the time for updates.

options.t: Approval process
options.why: Choosing the time for updates is not a sign-off on whether they may happen.

options.t: Standard operating procedure
options.why: An SOP lists the steps of a routine task; the manager chose a time.

options.t: Maintenance window
options.why: A pre-scheduled time of low activity for making changes is a maintenance window.

detail: The clubs are closed then and the booking site has almost no visitors
explain: A maintenance window is a pre-scheduled, low-impact time for changes, often overnight or at weekends.

stem: The e-commerce lead at a gift basket company blocks all non-emergency changes to the web store from December 1 to January 2, the busiest weeks of the year.
ask: Which of the following is the lead applying?

detail: the busiest weeks of the year
explain: A change freeze blocks routine changes during a critical business period such as peak season, when disruption would cost the most.

stem: An operations manager at an online bookstore runs the catalog database upgrade in the agreed window from 01:00 to 04:00 on Sunday. At 03:30 the upgrade is only half done, and the remaining work needs about two more hours. Nothing has failed, and the tested backout takes 25 minutes.
ask: What should the manager do?

options.t: Start the backout so it ends by 04:00
options.why: Work starts and ends inside the window. Work that cannot finish is backed out before the window closes.

options.t: Keep working past 04:00 until it is done
options.why: The window ends at 04:00. Running two hours past it disrupts the people the window was chosen to protect.

options.t: Leave it half done and skip the backout
options.why: A half-finished upgrade leaves the database in an untested state when the window closes.

options.t: Treat the rest as an emergency change
options.why: Nothing urgent threatens the business. Running out of time on a planned change is not an emergency.

detail: the remaining work needs about two more hours
explain: A maintenance window is the scheduled time for the work. If the work cannot finish inside it, the backout runs before the window closes, and the change is tried again in a later window.

stem: A software firm with offices in Tokyo, Berlin and Chicago finds there is no hour when nobody is working. Its change manager sets a separate time for changes to each region's servers, during that region's night.

options.why: No way to undo a change is described.

options.t: Maintenance windows
options.why: Scheduled low-activity times for changes, here one per region, are maintenance windows.

options.t: Restricted activities
options.why: Restricted activities keep work inside an approved scope; they do not set times.

detail: during that region's night
explain: When there is no quiet hour for the whole company, maintenance windows are set per region or per system at each one's quietest time.

stem: On a Tuesday afternoon, a storage engineer at a utility billing provider sees the disk array of the main billing server starting to fail, and a vendor firmware fix will stop it. The next scheduled maintenance window is five days away.
ask: Which of the following is true of applying the fix now?

options.t: It needs no record because it is urgent

options.t: It cancels all future windows
options.why: One emergency change does not change the regular schedule.

options.t: It may go outside the window if recorded
options.why: An emergency change can be made outside the window but must still be recorded and reviewed.

explain: Windows hold routine changes. An emergency change may happen outside one, but it is still recorded and reviewed afterward.

stem: A change manager at a call center outsourcer turns down a request to restart the phone platform at 10:00 on a Monday. She suggests 02:00 on Sunday instead, though the work and its risk are exactly the same.
ask: Which change management element is the manager applying?

options.why: The stem says the risk is exactly the same; only the time changes.

options.why: Nothing about undoing the restart is discussed.

options.t: Test results
options.why: No evidence from a test is mentioned; the decision is about timing.

stem: A change coordinator at an accounting software vendor checks a routine request against the policy lines below.

stem: A new change coordinator at a commercial printing company drafts the rules for when production changes may be made.
ask: Which of the following fit a maintenance window? (Select TWO)

options.t: Set in advance at a low-use time

options.why: A window is set in advance, not picked on the day by whoever does the work.

options.t: Often overnight or at weekends
options.why: Windows are commonly overnight or at weekends, when activity is lowest.

options.t: Placed in the busiest sales weeks
options.why: The busiest weeks are when changes are frozen, not when they are scheduled.

options.t: Used only after a change fails
options.why: A window is for making planned changes; undoing a failed one is the backout plan.

explain: Maintenance windows are pre-scheduled, low-impact times, often overnight or at weekends, so changes disrupt as few people as possible.

ask: Which of the following describes a standard operating procedure?

options.t: A written set of steps for a routine task

options.t: A scheduled quiet time for changes
options.why: A scheduled quiet time for changes is a maintenance window.

options.why: A documented way to undo a change is a backout plan.

ask: Which of the following statements about an SOP is accurate?

options.t: It covers only emergency changes
options.why: An SOP describes routine tasks, including the normal change process.

options.t: It must be updated when the process changes
options.why: An SOP has to match the current process, so it is updated whenever the process changes.

options.t: It takes the place of approval
options.why: An SOP can describe who approves a change; it does not replace the approval.

stem: A new technician at an armored transport company adds user accounts to the dispatch system exactly as senior staff do. He follows a numbered, written checklist that the team keeps on its wiki.

stem: The change coordinator at a hot sauce maker publishes a document that explains how to submit a change request, who signs it off and how to record the result. Every team now handles changes the same way.

options.why: The document says nothing about when changes happen.

options.why: Documented steps for submitting, approving and recording changes are a standard operating procedure (SOP) for the change process itself.

detail: explains how to submit a change request, who signs it off and how to record the result
explain: An SOP can describe the change process itself: how to submit a request, who approves it and how the outcome is recorded.

stem: The IT lead at a regional theater group publishes recommended tips for writing change requests, which staff may follow or ignore. An auditor says the team still lacks required, step-by-step instructions for the request process.

options.t: A change management policy
options.why: A policy states what must happen and why. The auditor wants the required step-by-step instructions.

options.t: A standard operating procedure
options.why: Required, step-by-step instructions for a routine task are a standard operating procedure (SOP).

options.t: An incident response procedure
options.why: Incident response procedures cover handling incidents, not writing change requests.

detail: required, step-by-step instructions for the request process
explain: Tips that may be ignored form a guideline. Required step-by-step instructions for a routine task are a standard operating procedure.

stem: The IT operations manager at a data analytics firm asks the change board to pre-approve the monthly antivirus signature updates, so each one need not wait for a board meeting. The board agrees.

options.t: A documented update procedure

options.why: A vote on every update is what pre-approval replaces.

options.t: An emergency change procedure

stem: An auditor at a logistics software company asks three backup operators how they restore a deleted shared folder for a user. She gets three different methods, and one of them never checks that the restored files open.

options.t: A longer maintenance window

stem: A new project manager at a hydroelectric utility asks which document gives the exact steps for submitting a change request and recording its result. The company also has a security policy stating that every change must be approved, and why.
