options.why: The firewall permits only listed addresses, so the new address had to be added as part of the change.

options.why: More time would not help; the firewall would still block the unlisted address.

options.t: A new owner for the change
options.why: Who owns the change does not affect what the firewall permits.

options.t: A second approval vote
options.why: Another sign-off would not add the address to the firewall list.

detail: permits outbound traffic only to addresses on its list
explain: A change can be blocked by a list it did not update. Adding the new address to the allow list belonged in the same change.

stem: An approved update leaves the inventory app at a model train retailer blocked by the application control tool. To get it working quickly, a technician edits the rule to permit every program in the app's folder, including files nobody has reviewed.
ask: Which risk of list changes does this show?

options.t: A list blocking the updated app
options.why: The edit removed the block; the problem now is what else it permits.

options.t: An update that skipped approval
options.why: The stem says the update was approved.

options.t: A list edit opening unwanted access
options.why: Permitting every file in the folder lets unreviewed programs run, an opening nobody intended.

options.t: A restart that interrupts users
options.why: No restart is mentioned; the issue is what the edited rule now permits.

detail: including files nobody has reviewed
explain: List updates can break access or open it. A broad edit made to fix a block can quietly let unreviewed programs run.

source.chapter: Allow lists and deny lists in change management

stem: The IT manager at an airport lounge operator wants the guest kiosks to run only the web browser and the boarding pass printer app. Every other program must be blocked, including programs nobody has seen before.
ask: Which of the following should the manager configure?

options.t: Deny list
options.why: A deny list blocks only listed programs, so a program nobody has seen before would still run.

options.t: Antivirus
options.why: Antivirus looks for known malware; it does not limit the kiosks to two programs.

options.t: Sandboxing
options.why: Sandboxing runs programs in isolation; it does not stop other programs from running.

options.t: Allow list
options.why: An allow list permits only the two listed programs and denies everything else, including unknown ones.

detail: including programs nobody has seen before
explain: Only an allow list denies everything not listed, so it blocks programs nobody has seen before. A deny list would let those run.

source.chapter: Allow lists and deny lists in change management

stem: The IT lead at a craft supply chain blocks five known gambling programs on staff computers and lets everything else run, so that new tools staff install keep working. A reviewer is asked to note the main weakness of this setup.
ask: Which of the following should the reviewer note?

options.t: Every new tool is blocked by default
options.why: That describes an allow list. Here everything not listed runs.

options.t: A new unwanted program runs until listed
options.why: A deny list blocks only what is on it, so anything new and unwanted runs until someone adds it.

options.t: The five listed programs can still run
options.why: The listed programs are exactly the ones this deny list blocks.

options.t: It cannot block any program at all
options.why: It blocks the five listed programs.

detail: lets everything else run
explain: A deny list blocks the listed items and lets everything else run. It is easy to live with but misses anything new.

source.chapter: Allow lists and deny lists in change management

stem: After retiring the old payroll server at 203.0.113.40, a network engineer at a staffing software firm leaves that address on the firewall allow list for the payroll database. The address may later be given to another system.
ask: Which of the following is the risk of leaving the entry?

options.t: The firewall will let a stranger in
options.why: An entry the change made obsolete still permits access, so whatever later uses that address is let in.

options.t: The new payroll server will be blocked
options.why: The stale entry does not block anything; it permits the old address.

options.t: The firewall will deny all payroll traffic
options.why: Leaving an extra allowed address does not make the firewall deny everything.

options.t: The database will need a restart
options.why: A stale list entry does not require any restart.

detail: The address may later be given to another system
explain: Entries a change makes obsolete should be removed in the same change. Left in place, they turn into permanent holes in the list.

source.chapter: Allow lists and deny lists in change management

stem: The service desk manager at a research nonprofit gets approval for a new remote support tool. The web proxy blocks a list of domains, and the vendor's domain is still on that list from an old, resolved report. Everything else on the web is reachable.
ask: Which of the following must the change include for the tool to work?

options.t: Adding the domain to the deny list
options.why: The domain is already on the deny list; that is why the tool would be blocked.

options.t: A longer maintenance window
options.why: More time does not change what the proxy blocks.

options.t: Removing the domain from the deny list
options.why: The proxy blocks listed domains, so the vendor's domain must come off the deny list as part of the change.

options.t: A restart of every laptop
options.why: Restarting laptops does not change the proxy list that blocks the domain.

detail: the vendor's domain is still on that list
explain: A deny list blocks only what is on it. A change can be blocked by an old entry, so updating the list belongs in the change.

source.chapter: Allow lists and deny lists in change management

stem: The morning after an approved upgrade of the shift planning app at a home care agency, nobody can open it. A desktop engineer finds the entries below.
ask: Which of the following does the log show?

lines: 07:58:12   reason: no matching allow entry (hash changed)

options.t: The app depends on a stopped service
options.why: The log names the reason: no matching allow entry, not a stopped service.

options.t: The new version is not on the allow list
options.why: The tool blocks version 6.0 because its changed hash has no allow entry.

options.t: The allow list now blocks every app
options.why: The mail client is still permitted, so only the upgraded app is blocked.

options.t: The upgrade ran outside its window
options.why: Nothing in the log is about timing; it shows a block by the list.

detail: reason: no matching allow entry (hash changed)
explain: The upgrade changed the program file, and the allow list was not updated to match, so the tool blocks it. Other programs still run.

source.chapter: Allow lists and deny lists in change management

stem: A security analyst at a container leasing company prepares the list checks for a change that moves the partner VPN to a new gateway.
ask: Which of the following statements about lists in this change are accurate? (Select TWO)

options.t: The new gateway address may need adding
options.why: A change can need a list updated, such as permitting the new gateway address.

options.t: List edits need no review of their own
options.why: A list edit can open access, so it is reviewed as part of the change.

options.t: A deny list blocks everything not listed
options.why: A deny list blocks only listed items; everything else runs.

options.t: Old entries the change retires should go
options.why: Entries the change makes obsolete should be removed, or they become openings.

options.t: An allow list permits anything not listed
options.why: An allow list denies everything not on it.

detail: moves the partner VPN to a new gateway
explain: Changes often need list updates: add what the change brings in, remove what it retires, and review the edit, since a careless list edit can open access.

source.chapter: Allow lists and deny lists in change management

ask: Which of the following describes restricted activities during a change?

options.t: Scheduling the work for a quiet business period
options.why: That describes a maintenance window, which sets when work happens, not what may be done.

options.t: Undoing the work if it causes problems
options.why: That describes a backout plan, which returns the system to its previous state.

options.t: Staying within the work that was approved
options.why: Restricted activities means the implementer does only the approved work and makes no unapproved extra changes.

options.t: Rating the risk of the work before sign-off
options.why: That describes impact analysis, which happens before approval, not a limit on the work itself.

explain: Restricted activities keeps the real change identical to the approved one: anything outside the approved scope needs its own approval.

ask: Which change management term covers the rule that an implementer may not add unapproved extra work while carrying out an approved change?

options.t: Restricted activities
options.why: This term limits the implementer to the approved scope.

options.t: Backout plan
options.why: A backout plan is a way to undo a change, not a limit on what the implementer may do.

options.t: Maintenance window
options.why: A maintenance window is the time set aside for changes, not a limit on their content.

options.t: Downtime
options.why: Downtime is the period a service is unavailable, not a rule about extra work.

explain: Restricted activities is the change management rule that the implementer stays inside the approved scope; widening the scope needs new approval.

stem: A database administrator at a seed bank is approved to add an index to one table. While working, she notices that a second table grants read access to far more staff than it should.
ask: What should the administrator do about the second table?

options.t: Tighten its access while she is logged in
options.why: Tightening access now is unapproved extra work, even though it would improve security.

options.t: List it in this change's backout plan
options.why: Listing it in the backout plan does not approve the fix; it is still outside this change.

options.t: Add it to this change's scope herself
options.why: Widening the scope needs new approval; she cannot widen it herself.

options.t: Raise a separate change request for it
options.why: Work outside the approved scope needs its own approved change, so she records it as a new request.

detail: approved to add an index to one table
explain: The approval covered one index on one table. A problem found elsewhere becomes its own change request, so it gets its own analysis, testing and approval.

stem: During an approved firmware upgrade on a hospital's nurse call server, a systems engineer also turned off an unused remote access feature he spotted. The change record lists only the firmware upgrade.
ask: Which of the following change management requirements did the engineer fail to follow?

options.t: Backout plan
options.why: Nothing in the stem concerns how to undo the upgrade; the problem is the extra work he did.

options.t: Restricted activities
options.why: He did work beyond the approved firmware upgrade, which breaks the limit to the approved scope.

options.t: Maintenance window
options.why: The stem gives no sign the work happened at the wrong time; it was done during the approved change.

options.t: Stakeholders
options.why: The stem says nothing about affected groups being left out; it describes an unapproved extra step.

detail: also turned off an unused remote access feature
explain: Even a helpful security fix is outside the scope when it is not in the approved change. It needed its own request.

stem: A storage administrator at a law firm is approved to move a file share to a new server. The move stops because the new server's disk quota is too small to hold the share. Firm policy allows a small extra step, recorded in the change, when the approved task cannot be finished without it.
ask: What should the administrator do?

options.t: Raise the quota and leave it out of the change record
options.why: The policy requires the extra step to be recorded in the change.

options.t: Raise the quota and log that step in the change
options.why: The policy allows this minimal extra step because the approved move cannot finish without it, as long as it is recorded.

options.t: Raise the quota and also tidy the share's folders
options.why: Tidying the folders is not needed to finish the move, so it is outside the approved scope.

options.t: Raise the quota and move a second share as well
options.why: A second share was never approved and is not needed to finish this move.

detail: when the approved task cannot be finished without it
explain: Some policies allow a small extra change only when the approved task cannot be finished without it. Anything beyond that, or anything unrecorded, breaks the scope limit.

stem: A change manager at a shipping insurer tells new technicians that they must not make "while I am in there" fixes during approved work, even small ones.
ask: Which of the following risks does the manager's rule reduce?

options.t: Users losing unsaved work when a program closes
options.why: That is the risk of an application restart, which this rule does not address.

options.t: A new program blocked by the allow list
options.why: That comes from allow and deny lists not being updated, not from extra fixes.

options.t: An old unsupported system breaking after a change
options.why: That is the risk of legacy applications, which this rule does not address.

options.t: Side effects from edits nobody analyzed or tested
options.why: An extra fix skips impact analysis, testing and the backout plan, so its side effects are unknown.

detail: must not make "while I am in there" fixes
explain: Staying inside the approved scope protects against untested side effects: only the analyzed, tested and approved work is done.

stem: A change manager at a pharmaceutical distributor reviews what an implementer did during an approved patch of the order server.
ask: Which of the following actions respected the limits of the approved change? (Select TWO)

options.t: Restarting the order server as the patch required
options.why: A restart the approved patch needs is part of the approved work.

options.t: Restarting the warehouse server to clear a fault
options.why: The warehouse server was not part of the approved patch.

options.t: Recording a fault found elsewhere as a new request
options.why: Recording a separate finding for its own change is how scope is respected.

options.t: Updating the backup agent while connected
options.why: The backup agent update was not approved in this change.

options.t: Opening a firewall port the patch did not need
options.why: A port the patch did not need is unapproved extra work.

detail: during an approved patch of the order server
explain: Only the approved patch, with what it needs such as its restart, is in scope. A problem found elsewhere is written up as its own request rather than fixed on the spot.

stem: A change auditor at a regional theater chain reads the implementation notes below.
ask: Which of the following entries falls outside the approved work?

lines: CHG-3318 scope: replace TLS certificate on web03.example only
21:06 web03.example web daemon restarted, status active

options.t: The 21:09 entry
options.why: web04 and its SSH port are not in the scope line, which names only the certificate on web03.

options.t: The 21:02 entry
options.why: Replacing the certificate on web03 is exactly the approved work.

options.t: The 21:06 entry
options.why: Restarting the web daemon on web03 is needed for the new certificate to take effect.

options.t: The 21:15 entry
options.why: Signing off ends the change; it is not extra work.

detail: 21:09 web04.example SSH port changed to 2222
explain: The scope line limits the change to one certificate on one server. Changing another server's SSH port needed its own approved change.

stem: An auditor at a hotel chain reads two rules in the IT handbook. Rule 1 says staff may not install games on work laptops. Rule 2 says that while carrying out a change, technicians touch only the systems and settings named in the approved request.
ask: Which of the following correctly describes the two rules?

options.t: Rule 1 is restricted activities; rule 2 is acceptable use
options.why: Rule 1 governs everyday laptop use, which is acceptable use. Restricted activities limit work during a change.

options.t: Both rules are restricted activities
options.why: Only rule 2 is about change work. Rule 1 covers everyday use of laptops.

options.t: Rule 1 is acceptable use; rule 2 is restricted activities
options.why: Keeping change work to what the approval names is restricted activities. A ban on games for everyday use is acceptable use.

options.t: Both rules are acceptable use
options.why: Rule 2 limits what technicians do while carrying out a change, which is restricted activities.

detail: touch only the systems and settings named in the approved request
explain: Restricted activities is about staying inside the approved scope during a change, not about forbidden activities in general, which an acceptable use policy covers.

stem: Two days after an approved change to a bakery chain's point-of-sale server, card payments fail. The change record lists only a receipt printer setting, so the incident team spends hours testing that setting before a technician admits he also edited the payment gateway address.
ask: Which of the following problems does this show when an implementer goes beyond the approved work?

options.t: The maintenance window becomes too short
options.why: Nothing in the stem shows the window ran short; the delay came from a misleading record.

options.t: The service restart fails to complete
options.why: No restart failure is described; the payments failed because of the extra edit.

options.t: The stakeholders cannot be identified
options.why: The stem does not mention any trouble finding affected groups.

options.t: The investigators chase the wrong cause
options.why: The record named only the printer setting, so the team chased it instead of the unrecorded gateway edit.

detail: he also edited the payment gateway address
explain: An unapproved extra change is missing from the change record, so investigators look at the approved work first and lose time.

ask: Which of the following describes downtime in change management?

options.t: The scheduled slot set aside for making changes
options.why: That is a maintenance window: when work is scheduled, not the outage itself.

options.t: The period in which no changes are allowed at all
options.why: That is a change freeze, which blocks changes during critical business periods.

options.t: The time a service is out of use because of a change
options.why: Downtime is the period a service is unavailable because of a change.

options.t: The record of who approved a change and when
options.why: That is part of the approval process, not a period of unavailability.

explain: Downtime is the outage a change causes. It should be planned, kept short and announced.

ask: Which change management term names the time a system cannot be used while a change is carried out?

options.t: Maintenance window
options.why: A maintenance window is when work is scheduled; the system is not necessarily unusable for all of it.

options.t: Downtime
options.why: Downtime is the time the system is unavailable because of the change.

options.t: Backout plan
options.why: A backout plan describes how to undo a change, not a period of unavailability.

options.t: Restricted activities
options.why: Restricted activities limits the work to the approved scope; it is not a period of time.

explain: Downtime is the outage itself, while the maintenance window is the time slot it is scheduled into.

stem: A security analyst at a property management firm sees the rent portal stop answering at 09:00 on a Thursday and opens an incident for a possible attack. An hour later she learns the IT team had taken the portal offline for an approved upgrade.
ask: Which of the following would have prevented the false alarm?

options.t: Announcing the outage in advance
options.why: Planned downtime is announced to the people it affects. Had the analyst known, the outage would not have looked like an attack.

options.t: Keeping the upgrade within its scope
options.why: The stem describes no extra work; the portal was taken offline for the approved upgrade itself.

options.t: Updating the allow list for the release
options.why: Nothing was blocked by a list; the portal was taken offline on purpose.

options.t: Writing a way to undo the upgrade
options.why: A way to undo the upgrade would not have told the analyst the outage was planned.

detail: opens an incident for a possible attack
explain: Planned downtime must be announced to the people it affects, including the security team. Unannounced downtime floods the help desk and can look like an attack.

stem: A web developer at a science museum sets the ticket shop to show a page saying sales will return at 10:30 while the shop is being upgraded, instead of a browser error.
ask: What is the purpose of this page?

options.t: Telling visitors about a planned outage
options.why: A maintenance page communicates downtime so visitors know the shop is unavailable and when it returns.

options.t: Limiting the work to the approved scope
options.why: A page shown to visitors does not limit what the developer changes.

options.t: Recording who approved the work
options.why: Approval records live in the change system, not on a page shown to visitors.

options.t: Undoing the work if it fails
options.why: Undoing the work is the backout plan; the page does nothing to the upgrade itself.

detail: sales will return at 10:30
explain: A maintenance page is a common way to communicate planned downtime to the people who would otherwise see an error.

stem: A database administrator at an online grocer upgrades the order database by first moving all traffic to a standby copy, upgrading the primary, then moving traffic back, so shoppers can keep ordering throughout.
ask: Which technical implication is this approach designed to reduce?

options.t: Dependencies
options.why: The stem does not describe other systems that must change; it describes keeping one store available.

options.t: Downtime
options.why: Failing over to a standby copy keeps the store usable, which reduces downtime.

options.t: Service restart
options.why: The primary is still upgraded and restarted; the approach does not remove that, it keeps shoppers served meanwhile.

options.t: Legacy applications
options.why: Nothing in the stem is old or unsupported.

detail: so shoppers can keep ordering throughout
explain: Redundancy and failover are the usual ways to reduce downtime: traffic moves to a working copy while the change is made.

stem: An infrastructure engineer at a city parking agency plans to keep the parking payment site up during a server upgrade by sending its traffic to a second data center. That second site has never carried live traffic.
ask: What should the engineer do before the upgrade?

options.t: Book the upgrade for the busiest hour
options.why: If anything goes wrong, the busiest hour does the most harm. Changes go into quiet times.

options.t: Test the switch to the second site
options.why: Failover reduces downtime only if it works. A site that has never carried live traffic is tested before the change relies on it.

options.t: Drop the backout since traffic moves
options.why: The upgrade can still fail. Moving traffic away does not undo a failed upgrade.

options.t: Tell users only if the switch fails
options.why: Users and the help desk are told about the work in advance, whatever the plan.

detail: That second site has never carried live traffic
explain: Failover to a second site reduces downtime, but only if it works. It is tested before a change depends on it.

stem: The infrastructure lead at a ride-hailing company must upgrade the dispatch servers and keep any outage riders see as short as possible.
ask: Which of the following steps meet this goal? (Select TWO)

options.t: Fail traffic over to a second site during the work
options.why: Failover keeps dispatch running elsewhere, so riders see little or no outage.

options.t: Restart every server at once to save time
options.why: Restarting all servers together takes the whole service down at once.

options.t: Upgrade one node at a time behind the load balancer
options.why: The other nodes keep serving while one is upgraded, which reduces the outage.

options.t: Add unrelated fixes so fewer windows are needed
options.why: Extra fixes add untested work and risk; they do not shorten what riders see.

options.t: Tell users about the work only after it is done
options.why: Late notice does not shorten the outage, and downtime should be announced in advance.

detail: keep any outage riders see as short as possible
explain: Redundancy and failover reduce downtime: traffic is served by another site or node while each part is upgraded.

stem: A site reliability engineer at an online florist reviews the load balancer log below from last night's patching of the two shop servers.
ask: What customer-facing outage did the patching cause, based on the log?

lines: 22:00 lb1 pool shop: webA drained, webB serving
22:14 lb1 pool shop: webA healthy, back in pool
22:15 lb1 pool shop: webB drained, webA serving
22:29 lb1 pool shop: webB healthy, back in pool

options.t: 14 minutes
options.why: That is how long each server was out of the pool, but the other server served customers each time.

options.t: 28 minutes
options.why: That adds both servers' time out of the pool, but the other server served customers each time.

options.t: 29 minutes
options.why: That is the length of the whole job, not time when customers had no server.

options.t: 0 minutes
options.why: One server was always serving: webB while webA was patched, then webA while webB was patched.

detail: 22:15 lb1 pool shop: webB drained, webA serving
explain: Patching one node at a time behind a load balancer is a way to avoid customer-facing downtime: the other node carries the traffic.

stem: A change coordinator at a ferry operator files a request for the booking system that reads: "Window: Tuesday 23:00 to 01:00. Booking site offline 23:15 to 23:45 during the database upgrade."
ask: Which of the following BEST describes the 30 minutes when the booking site is offline?

options.t: Maintenance window
options.why: The window is the two-hour slot from 23:00 to 01:00; the offline half hour sits inside it but is not the window.

options.t: Downtime
options.why: The 30 minutes when the site cannot be used is the downtime the change causes.

options.t: Backout plan
options.why: A backout plan is how to undo the change; the request line describes an outage.

options.t: Service restart
options.why: The request names no restart; it states when the site is unavailable.

detail: Booking site offline 23:15 to 23:45
edge: The window is the scheduled slot for the work; the part of it when the site is unusable is the downtime.
explain: Downtime is the outage itself; the maintenance window is the time it is scheduled into, here two hours that contain the 30 minutes.

stem: A risk analyst at a county library rates each planned change by the security goal it threatens. One change takes the catalog site offline for an hour, but no data is exposed or altered.
ask: Which security goal does the analyst mark as affected?

options.t: Confidentiality
options.why: No data is exposed, so confidentiality is not affected.

options.t: Integrity
options.why: No data is altered, so integrity is not affected.

options.t: Availability
options.why: Downtime makes the catalog site unusable for an hour, which affects availability.

options.t: Non-repudiation
options.why: Nothing in the stem concerns proving who did an action.

detail: no data is exposed or altered
explain: Downtime affects availability, the A of the CIA triad. The stem rules out confidentiality and integrity.

ask: Which of the following describes a service restart in change management?

options.t: Closing and reopening a program people have open
options.why: That describes an application restart, which concerns programs users interact with.

options.t: Rebooting every device on a network segment
options.why: A service restart concerns one background service, not every device on a segment.

options.t: Returning a system to its state before a change
options.why: That describes a backout, which undoes a change rather than applying it.

options.t: Stopping and starting a background process for a change
options.why: A service restart stops and starts a background service or daemon so a change takes effect.

explain: A service restart applies a change to a background service or daemon. It can briefly interrupt anything using that service.

ask: Which term names stopping and starting a daemon so that a configuration change takes effect?

options.t: Service restart
options.why: Stopping and starting a daemon so a change applies is a service restart.

options.t: Application restart
options.why: An application restart closes and reopens a program users have open, not a daemon.

options.t: Backout plan
options.why: A backout plan undoes a change; it does not make a change take effect.

options.t: Downtime
options.why: Downtime is a period of unavailability, which a restart may cause, not the act of restarting.

explain: Daemons are background services, so restarting one to apply a change is a service restart.

stem: A systems administrator at a regional airport edits the time server's settings file to use a new upstream source. The time daemon reads that file only when it starts, and clients still get time from the old source.
ask: What must the administrator do for the edit to take effect?

options.t: Reboot every client computer
options.why: The clients are not the problem; the daemon has not loaded its new settings.

options.t: Have users reopen their programs
options.why: The time daemon is a background process; reopening user programs does not reload it.

options.t: Restart it so it loads the new file
options.why: The daemon reads its settings only at start, so it must be stopped and started again.

options.t: Roll back the settings file
options.why: Rolling back would undo the edit instead of making it take effect.

detail: reads that file only when it starts
explain: Many configuration changes apply only after the service restarts. Here the daemon reads its settings at start, so a service restart is needed.

stem: A server engineer at a university restarts the directory service, which checks every staff and student login, to load a new certificate. The university has only one directory server.
ask: What will staff and students notice while the service restarts?

options.t: A brief break in signing in
options.why: A restart interrupts anything using the service. With one directory server, logins cannot be checked until it is back.

options.t: Loss of their unsaved documents
options.why: Lost unsaved work comes from closing a program people have open, not from a background service restarting.

options.t: No effect, as it runs in the background
options.why: Running in the background does not hide it: every login depends on it while it is down.

options.t: A change to their access rights
options.why: Loading a certificate does not change what anyone may access.

detail: which checks every staff and student login
explain: A service restart can interrupt anything using the service. A sole directory server going down for a moment pauses every login, so the restart is planned for a quiet time.

stem: A database administrator at a tax firm changes a memory setting for the database engine, which runs in the background on a server. Staff never open the engine directly, and the setting applies only when the engine is stopped and started again.
ask: Which technical implication must the change plan include?

options.t: Application restart
options.why: Staff never open the engine, so it is not a user-facing program.

options.t: Legacy applications
options.why: Nothing in the stem says the engine is old or unsupported.

options.t: Restricted activities
options.why: The stem describes no work beyond the approved setting change.

options.t: Service restart
options.why: The engine is a background process that must be stopped and started, which is a service restart.

detail: Staff never open the engine directly
explain: A background database engine is a service. Applying the setting means restarting it, which should be planned and checked.

source.chapter: Technical implications of a change compared (allow lists, scope, downtime, restarts, legacy, dependencies)

stem: After an approved update, the logging agent on a law firm's file server is restarted. Two days later, an analyst notices that the server has sent no security events since the update.
ask: Which of the following should the post-change check have confirmed?

options.t: That users had saved their open files
options.why: Saving files concerns user programs; the problem is a background agent that stopped.

options.t: That the agent came back and is running
options.why: A restarted agent can fail to start, leaving a silent gap; checking it was running would have caught this.

options.t: That the agent was on the deny list
options.why: A deny list blocks software; putting the agent there would stop it, which is the problem here.

options.t: That the server's drawing was up to date
options.why: An accurate drawing would not show whether the agent restarted.

detail: has sent no security events since the update
explain: Security services must be checked after a restart too: an agent that fails to start quietly leaves attacks unseen.

stem: A database administrator at a payroll firm plans an upgrade of the database engine that requires restarting it. The payroll job daemon, which connects to the database when it starts, must also be restarted or it keeps failing.
ask: Which restart order should the change plan specify?

options.t: Payroll job daemon first, then the database engine
options.why: The daemon would start while the database is still down and fail to connect.

options.t: Database engine first, then the payroll job daemon
options.why: The job daemon connects when it starts, so the database must already be back.

options.t: Both at the same moment
options.why: Starting both together lets the daemon try to connect before the database is ready.

options.t: Only the database engine
options.why: The stem says the payroll daemon must also be restarted or it keeps failing.

detail: which connects to the database when it starts
explain: When services depend on each other, the change plan restarts them in order: the one being relied on first.

stem: A mail administrator at a freight forwarder changes a relay setting and then runs the commands below.
ask: What does this output show about the change?

lines: postfix: fatal: bad parameter in main.cf line 42

options.t: The change is live and working
options.why: The daemon reports failed, so nothing is live.

options.t: Users must close and reopen their mail program
options.why: The failure is in the background mail daemon, not in a program users have open.

options.t: A firewall rule blocked the mail daemon
options.why: The journal names a bad setting on line 42, not a blocked connection.

options.t: The mail daemon did not come back after restarting
options.why: is-active reports failed and the journal shows a fatal settings error, so the daemon did not start.

detail: postfix: fatal: bad parameter in main.cf line 42
explain: A service restart can fail to come back cleanly. Checking its status after the restart shows the change broke the mail service.

stem: A systems administrator at a hotel chain writes a change plan to restart the reservation system's background database process overnight.
ask: Which of the following belong in the plan? (Select TWO)

options.t: Warn the night front desk before the restart
options.why: The restart briefly interrupts what uses the database, so the people affected should be warned.

options.t: Schedule it for the busiest check-in hour
options.why: A restart should be scheduled for low use, not the busiest hour.

options.t: Check the process is healthy after the restart
options.why: A service may not come back cleanly, so it is verified afterward.

options.t: Skip planning, since restarts are routine
options.why: A restart carries outage risk and should be planned, not skipped.

options.t: Ask guests to save their work first
options.why: Guests do not use the background database directly; saving work concerns user programs.

detail: restart the reservation system's background database process
explain: A service restart is planned: people who rely on the service are warned, and the service is checked once it is back.

stem: A broadcast engineer at a radio station changes the listener limit in the streaming software's settings file. The software runs as a background service on a server that also hosts the music library and the ad scheduler. A colleague proposes rebooting the whole server to apply the change.
ask: Which of the following does the full reboot cause that a restart of only the streaming service would not?

options.t: Every other service on it stops too
options.why: A reboot stops and starts every service on the server, the music library and ad scheduler included; a service restart touches only the streaming software.

options.t: The streaming service ignores the change
options.why: A reboot starts the streaming service again, so it reads the new setting just as a service restart would.

options.t: The settings file is rolled back
options.why: Neither a reboot nor a service restart rolls back a settings file.

options.t: Staff lose unsaved desktop work
options.why: The software runs as a background service on a server, not on anyone's desktop.

detail: also hosts the music library and the ad scheduler
explain: A service restart stops and starts one background service. A full reboot restarts every service on the server, so restarting just the one service applies the change with less disruption.

ask: Which of the following describes an application restart during a change?

options.t: Stopping and starting a background daemon
options.why: That is a service restart, which concerns background processes, not programs users have open.

options.t: Reinstalling a program's earlier release
options.why: Going back to an earlier release is a backout, not a restart to apply an update.

options.t: Closing and reopening a user program so an update applies
options.why: An application restart closes and reopens a program users work in so the change takes effect.

options.t: Moving users to a standby server
options.why: Moving users to a standby server is failover, used to reduce downtime.

explain: An application restart affects users directly: the program they have open closes and reopens, and unsaved work can be lost.

ask: Which term names closing and reopening a desktop program on each workstation so its update takes effect?

options.t: Service restart
options.why: A service restart is for background services, not desktop programs.

options.t: Legacy applications
options.why: Legacy applications are old, often unsupported programs; the term is not about reopening one.

options.t: Downtime
options.why: Downtime is a period of unavailability, not the act of reopening a program.

options.t: Application restart
options.why: Closing and reopening a program users work in is an application restart.

explain: A desktop program is something users have open, so restarting it to apply an update is an application restart.

stem: The IT coordinator at an architecture firm pushes an update to the drafting program on 60 workstations. The update takes effect only after each designer closes and reopens the program.
ask: What should the coordinator do before the program is closed for the update?

options.t: Restart the file server's background daemons
options.why: The update is to a desktop program; the file server's daemons are not involved.

options.t: Add the update to the deny list
options.why: A deny list would block the update instead of letting it take effect.

options.t: Warn staff to save their drawings first
options.why: Closing the program can lose unsaved work, so staff are warned to save first.

options.t: Revise the network map
options.why: A desktop program update does not change the network layout.

detail: closes and reopens the program
explain: An application restart affects users directly and can lose unsaved data, so users are told to save their work before the program closes.

stem: A help desk manager at a marketing agency learns that after Friday's update, staff must close and reopen the email client on their laptops, and any unsaved draft will be lost.
ask: Which technical implication does this describe?

options.t: Service restart
options.why: The email client is a program staff have open, not a background service.

options.t: Application restart
options.why: Staff must close and reopen a program they use, which is an application restart.

options.t: Dependencies
options.why: The stem does not describe one system relying on another.

options.t: Legacy applications
options.why: Nothing in the stem says the email client is old or unsupported.

detail: staff must close and reopen the email client
explain: Closing and reopening a program users have open, with the risk of losing unsaved work, is an application restart.

stem: A shift supervisor at a call center asks IT to restart the call-handling program only between calls, because agents type notes into it during every call.
ask: Which risk is the supervisor trying to avoid?

options.t: Loss of unsaved work
options.why: Restarting a program mid-call would close it while notes are still unsaved.

options.t: A background daemon failing to start
options.why: The program is one agents type into, not a background daemon.

options.t: A program blocked by the allow list
options.why: Nothing in the stem concerns a list blocking the program.

options.t: Work outside the approved scope
options.why: The request is about timing the restart, not about extra unapproved work.

detail: agents type notes into it during every call
explain: An application restart can lose unsaved data, so it is timed for when users have nothing unsaved.

stem: The desktop team at a university must apply a browser update to 3,000 lab and staff computers this week. The update needs the browser closed and reopened, and lectures must not be interrupted.
ask: Which approach to the restart meets both requirements?

options.t: Let users restart it themselves before a deadline
options.why: Users close it when convenient, so lectures are not interrupted, and the deadline gets the update applied this week.

options.t: Force it closed on every computer at 10:00
options.why: A forced close in the middle of the day would interrupt lectures.

options.t: Restart the web proxy daemon instead
options.why: Restarting a proxy daemon does not apply an update to the browser on each computer.

options.t: Wait until next semester to apply it
options.why: The update must be applied this week.

detail: lectures must not be interrupted
explain: Application restarts affect users directly. Letting users restart at a convenient time within a deadline avoids interrupting them while still applying the update.

stem: After an update and restart of the accounting program at a brewery, the finance lead notices that it no longer asks for a second sign-in factor. The setting had reverted to its default during the restart.
ask: Which post-restart check would have caught this?

options.t: Confirming the background daemons are running
options.why: The problem is a setting inside a user program, not a stopped daemon.

options.t: Confirming its security settings were kept
options.why: A program can reopen with default settings, so checking its security settings after the restart would catch this.

options.t: Confirming the network map is current
options.why: A current network map says nothing about a program's sign-in setting.

options.t: Confirming the change stayed in scope
options.why: The change stayed in scope; the restart reset a setting.

detail: The setting had reverted to its default
explain: After an application restart, check that the program opens and keeps its settings: a default setting can quietly weaken security.

stem: An office manager at a wholesale florist forwards the notice below to all staff.
ask: Which of the following technical implications does this notice BEST address?

lines: At 18:00 the ledger program installs an update and closes on its own.
Save open entries before 17:55. It reopens about 3 minutes later.

options.t: Downtime
options.why: The program is briefly unusable, but the notice centers on a program closing and the risk to unsaved entries.

options.t: Service restart
options.why: The ledger program is something staff have open, not a background service.

options.t: Application restart
options.why: The notice warns that a program staff have open will close and reopen, and tells them to save their entries.

options.t: Legacy applications
options.why: The notice says nothing about the program being old or unsupported.

detail: Save open entries before 17:55
edge: The three minutes are a side effect; what staff are told to act on is a user program closing, which risks unsaved entries.
explain: An application restart closes a program users have open and can lose unsaved work, so users are warned to save first.

stem: A change coordinator at a seafood processor sorts the upcoming changes by the kind of restart each one needs.
ask: Which of the following changes need an application restart? (Select TWO)

options.t: An update to the label designer staff open on their PCs
options.why: Staff have the label designer open, so it is closed and reopened: an application restart.

options.t: A new setting for the database engine on the server
options.why: The database engine runs in the background, so it needs a service restart.

options.t: A new certificate for the web server daemon
options.why: A daemon is a background service, so it needs a service restart.

options.t: An update to the email client on staff laptops
options.why: Staff have the email client open, so it is closed and reopened: an application restart.

options.t: A patch to the background backup agent
options.why: A background agent is a service, so it needs a service restart.

detail: by the kind of restart each one needs
explain: Programs people have open need an application restart; background engines, daemons and agents need a service restart.

stem: A help desk technician at a property insurer proposes rebooting every laptop to apply an update to the claims program, although the update only needs the program closed and reopened.
ask: Which of the following is the drawback of this proposal?

options.t: It leaves the old release running
options.why: A reboot also restarts the claims program, so the update does take effect.

options.t: It skips the background daemons
options.why: A reboot restarts every service as well, so nothing is skipped.

options.t: It removes the program from the allow list
options.why: Rebooting does not change any allow list.

options.t: It disrupts users more than needed
options.why: A reboot closes every program and signs users out, when only one program had to be reopened.

detail: only needs the program closed and reopened
explain: An operating system reboot restarts both services and programs. When only an application restart is needed, rebooting interrupts users more than the change requires.

ask: Which of the following describes a legacy application in change management?

options.t: A program that relies on another system to work
options.why: Relying on another system describes a dependency, not age or lack of support.

options.t: A program that is old, fragile and often unsupported
options.why: Legacy applications are older programs, often unsupported and poorly documented, that break easily.

options.t: A program that must be closed and reopened to update
options.why: That describes an application restart.

options.t: A program that runs only if it is on an approved list
options.why: That describes an allow list, which controls what may run.

explain: A legacy application is old, often unsupported and fragile, so changes around it carry extra risk.

ask: Which of the following explains why a change near a legacy application carries extra risk?

options.t: It always runs as a background daemon
options.why: Age says nothing about whether a program is a background daemon.

options.t: It must stay on the deny list
options.why: A program on a deny list would be blocked; legacy programs are in use.

options.t: It may be fragile, undocumented and unsupported
options.why: Legacy applications are often unsupported, poorly documented and fragile, so they break easily.

options.t: It has no users who could be affected
options.why: Legacy programs are often still used for important work.

explain: Changes around legacy applications are risky because no vendor may help, little is written down, and the program may not cope with anything new.

stem: A fleet manager at a bus company still uses a route scheduling program whose maker stopped issuing updates years ago, and whose settings are written down nowhere. IT plans to move the program to a new server.
ask: Which technical implication makes this move riskier than usual?

options.t: Restricted activities
options.why: The stem describes no work beyond what is planned.

options.t: Allow lists/deny lists
options.why: Nothing in the stem concerns a list blocking or allowing the program.

options.t: Application restart
options.why: Reopening a program after a move is routine; it is not what makes this move riskier.

options.t: Legacy applications
options.why: An old program with no vendor updates and no documentation is a legacy application, which needs extra care.

detail: whose maker stopped issuing updates years ago
explain: An unsupported, undocumented program is a legacy application: a move can break it and no vendor can help, so the plan needs extra care.

stem: A new systems engineer at a sawmill inherits an old, unsupported kiln control program that has no manual. She must plan a change to the PC it runs on.
ask: Which of the following should the engineer do before the change?

options.t: Record how it works and what it connects to
options.why: Legacy applications should be documented, since no manual or vendor can explain them.

options.t: Restart it to see whether it recovers
options.why: Testing a fragile program by restarting it in production risks breaking it.

options.t: Put it on the deny list
options.why: A deny list would block the program the sawmill still needs.

options.t: Make the change and watch for errors
options.why: Changing first leaves no understanding of the program if it breaks.

detail: has no manual
explain: With no vendor and no manual, the team must write down how a legacy application works before changing anything around it.

stem: The IT director at a credit union wants to freeze every change to an old, unsupported loan program for good, saying that if nothing is touched, nothing can break.
ask: Which of the following is the flaw in the director's plan?

options.t: It will need a service restart
options.why: Freezing changes means nothing restarts; that is not the flaw.

options.t: Its allow list will keep growing
options.why: Freezing changes adds nothing to any list.

options.t: Known flaws stay open with no fix
options.why: An unsupported program gets no fixes, so leaving it untouched leaves its known weaknesses open.

options.t: Users will lose unsaved work
options.why: No restart or close is planned, so no unsaved work is at risk.

detail: saying that if nothing is touched, nothing can break
explain: Legacy risk runs both ways: changing it may break it, and leaving it alone keeps its flaws open, so it needs compensating controls and a replacement plan.

stem: A network engineer at a textile mill replaces the print server with a modern one. The next day, a pattern-cutting program from the 1990s, unsupported for years, cannot print because it only works with the old server's print protocol.
ask: Which of the following BEST describes the technical implication the engineer missed?

options.t: Legacy applications
options.why: The stem stresses an old, unsupported program that cannot cope with the newer server.

options.t: Dependencies
options.why: The program relies on printing, but the stem stresses that it is old and can only use the old protocol.

options.t: Service restart
options.why: No restart is described; the program cannot work with the new server at all.

options.t: Restricted activities
options.why: The engineer did the planned replacement and nothing more.

detail: from the 1990s, unsupported for years
edge: A dependency is involved, but the clue is an old, unsupported program unable to handle a modern change, which points to legacy applications.
explain: Old, fragile programs often break when something around them is modernized. The stress on age and lack of support makes this a legacy application problem.

stem: The IT manager at a natural history museum plans to replace the disks in the server that runs an old, unsupported collection catalog program.
ask: Which of the following belong in the change plan because of the catalog program? (Select TWO)

options.t: Trial the change on a faithful copy of the server first
options.why: A fragile program may break, so the change is tried on a faithful copy before production.

options.t: Skip testing, since no vendor can help anyway
options.why: No vendor help is a reason to test more, not less.

options.t: Leave the program out of the impact analysis
options.why: Changes near a legacy program are treated as higher risk in the impact analysis.

options.t: Keep a tested way back to the current setup
options.why: A solid backout plan matters most when the program may not survive the change.

options.t: Add unrelated fixes to the program while it is down
options.why: Extra fixes add untested risk to a fragile program and fall outside the approved scope.

detail: old, unsupported collection catalog program
explain: Changes around a legacy application need special handling: test on a faithful copy where possible and keep a solid way back.

stem: A change manager at a fuel depot reads the asset record below before approving a network change near the system.
ask: Which of the following should the change manager ask the system owner to add?

lines: OS: release from 2009, no further updates
Maker: out of business, no support contract
Docs: none; behavior known only from observation

options.t: A support contract from its maker
options.why: The maker is out of business, so no support contract can be had.

options.t: A lower change risk rating
options.why: An unsupported, undocumented system is rightly rated high risk for changes around it.

options.t: The latest operating system updates
options.why: The record says the release gets no further updates.

options.t: A target date to retire it
options.why: The risk of a legacy system grows over time, so its handling includes planning its replacement, and the record shows none.

detail: Replacement: none planned
explain: Legacy systems are fragile and their risk grows over time, so their handling includes a plan to replace them. This record says no replacement is planned.

stem: A database team at a shipping firm plans to update a database driver on a shared server. An old, unsupported customs program also runs on that server, though the change does not touch it directly.
ask: How should the impact analysis rate the driver update?

options.t: Lower risk, since the old program is not changed
options.why: The program shares the server and may rely on the driver, so it can still break.

options.t: Higher risk, since the old program may break
options.why: Changes that touch a legacy application even indirectly are treated as higher risk.

options.t: No risk, since only a driver changes
options.why: A driver update on a shared server can affect every program on it.

options.t: Not rated, since drivers need no analysis
options.why: A driver update is a change too, and one near a legacy program needs its risk assessed, not skipped.

detail: An old, unsupported customs program also runs on that server
explain: Fragile, unsupported programs can break when anything around them changes, so even indirect changes near them are rated higher risk.

stem: A new IT intern at a dairy suggests leaving an old, unsupported milk-testing program out of the impact analysis because it is "just legacy." The program records the test result of every batch.
ask: Which of the following corrects the intern?

options.t: It is unsupported, so changes cannot affect it
options.why: Unsupported programs are fragile, so changes affect them more, not less.

options.t: It runs a critical process, so it needs extra care
options.why: The program records every batch's test result, so it is critical and needs more care, not less.

options.t: It is old, so it can be removed without notice
options.why: Removing a program that records every test result would stop a critical process.

options.t: It is a background daemon, so users never notice it
options.why: Nothing in the stem says it is a daemon, and its results are clearly used.

detail: The program records the test result of every batch
explain: Legacy does not mean unimportant: old programs often run critical work that nobody can easily replace, so they need extra care in change planning.

ask: Which of the following describes dependencies in change management?

options.t: Old components their vendor no longer supports
options.why: That describes legacy applications, which are about age and support, not relationships.

options.t: Limits that keep work inside the approved scope
options.why: That describes restricted activities.

options.t: Times when a component cannot be used
options.why: That describes downtime.

options.t: Links where one component needs another to work
options.why: A dependency is a relationship in which one component relies on another, so changing one can affect the other.

explain: Dependencies are relationships between components. Because of them, one change can force changes or restarts elsewhere, sometimes on other systems.

ask: When should the links between a system being changed and the systems that rely on it be mapped?

options.t: Before the change is approved
options.why: Dependencies are mapped before approval so the analysis and plan cover every affected system.

options.t: After the change is closed
options.why: Mapping after closure is too late to plan steps or warn other owners.

options.t: Only if the change fails
options.why: Waiting for a failure means the hidden link is found by an outage.

options.t: During the maintenance window
options.why: The window is for carrying out the change, which must already be planned and approved.

explain: A change can cascade to other systems, so dependencies are mapped before approval and the steps are ordered to match.

stem: A web team lead at a sporting goods retailer must move the checkout servers to a new payment gateway release. The new release accepts only connections made with a newer encryption library than the checkout servers have now.
ask: Which order of work should the plan use?

options.t: The gateway first, then the library on the checkout servers
options.why: Checkout would fail between the two steps, because the new gateway refuses the old library.

options.t: The gateway only, leaving the library as it is
options.why: The new release refuses the old library, so checkout would stop working.

options.t: The library on the checkout servers first, then the gateway
options.why: The gateway will refuse the old library, so the library must be upgraded before the gateway switches.

options.t: The library only, leaving the gateway as it is
options.why: The move to the new gateway release is required, so it cannot be left out.

detail: accepts only connections made with a newer encryption library
explain: When one component relies on another, the plan orders the steps: the part that is relied on is made ready first.

stem: A storage engineer at a newspaper moves the photo archive to a file server with a new name. That night, the page layout system's import job, which reads photos from the old server name, fails.
ask: Which technical implication did the change plan miss?

options.t: Legacy applications
options.why: Nothing in the stem says the layout system is old or unsupported.

options.t: Restricted activities
options.why: The engineer did the planned move and nothing more.

options.t: Service restart
options.why: The job failed because the photos moved, not because something failed to restart.

options.t: Dependencies
options.why: The import job relied on the archive's old location, so moving it broke another system.

detail: which reads photos from the old server name
explain: A change in one place can break a system elsewhere that relies on it. Mapping what uses the archive would have found the import job.

stem: Before approving a firewall rule change on a hospital's lab network, the change board learns that the nightly results feed to the patient portal also passes through that firewall.
ask: What should the board require before approval?

options.t: A test of the firewall rule on its own
options.why: Testing only the changed part misses the feed that relies on it.

options.t: A plan to fix the feed later if it breaks
options.why: Waiting for a break means patients lose results first; the link is known now.

options.t: A test of the feed with the new rule in place
options.why: The feed relies on the firewall, so the whole chain is tested, not only the changed rule.

options.t: A shorter maintenance window
options.why: A shorter window does not show whether the feed still works.

detail: also passes through that firewall
explain: When other systems rely on the thing being changed, the test covers the whole chain before approval.

stem: A middleware engineer at a shipping firm moves the message queue server to a new address. The warehouse scanners' sync agent and the billing batch job both send their messages through that queue, and each must be restarted to pick up the new address.
ask: Which of the following BEST explains why the scanner agent and the billing job must restart?

options.t: Service restart
options.why: Restarts do happen, but the stem explains them by the systems relying on the queue server.

options.t: Dependencies
options.why: Both rely on the queue server, so a change to it forces changes in them.

options.t: Legacy applications
options.why: Nothing in the stem is old or unsupported.

options.t: Downtime
options.why: Downtime may follow, but it does not explain why unchanged systems must restart.

detail: both send their messages through that queue
edge: The restarts are the effect; they are needed because both systems rely on the queue server that moved.
explain: A change to one component can force restarts in the components that rely on it. The stem gives that relationship as the reason, which is a dependency.

stem: An application owner at an outdoor gear retailer reads the entry below before an upgrade of db-pay02.
ask: Which of the following could the db-pay02 upgrade affect, based on the entry?

options.t: pay-api01 and the three systems that need it

options.t: pay-api01 alone, not the systems that need it
options.why: The entry shows three systems that need pay-api01, so a problem there reaches them too.

options.t: hsm01 and pay-api01, not the systems that need it
options.why: hsm01 is something pay-api01 needs; it does not rely on db-pay02. The three systems that need pay-api01 are left out.

options.t: web-shop alone, not pay-api01 or the others
options.why: pay-api01 relies on db-pay02 directly, and two more systems need pay-api01.

detail: pay-api01 requires: db-pay02, hsm01
