stem: A change manager at an electric co-op reviews a plan to replace the server that receives outage reports. Three other systems read data from that server.
ask: Which of the following belong in the plan because other systems rely on the server? (Select TWO)

options.t: Notify the owners of the systems that read from it
options.why: Owners of the systems that rely on it are affected, so they are told and involved.

options.t: Treat it as a pre-approved standard change
options.why: A replacement that three other systems rely on needs full review, not the routine pre-approved path.

options.t: Skip testing the systems that read from it
options.why: Those systems are exactly what must be tested along with the change.

options.t: Cover every affected system in the backout plan
options.why: If the change fails, all affected systems must be returned to working order, not only the server.

options.t: Fix other servers found during the work
options.why: Extra fixes are outside the approved scope and unrelated to these links.

detail: Three other systems read data from that server
explain: Dependent systems widen the plan: their owners are involved, they are tested, and the backout covers them too.

stem: Each night, a partner's system pulls a file from a retailer's SFTP server. The retailer's IT lead plans to move that server to a new address.
ask: Which of the following should the change plan include?

options.t: Informing the partner and testing its transfer
options.why: The partner's system relies on the server's address, so the partner must be told and the transfer tested.

options.t: Moving it quietly, since only internal staff use it
options.why: The stem says a partner's system uses it every night.

options.t: Restarting the partner's servers afterward
options.why: A restart does not tell the partner's system the new address.

options.t: Changing the address only on the network map
options.why: Updating a map does not keep the partner's nightly transfer working.

detail: a partner's system pulls a file
explain: Dependencies can be operational as well as technical: an outside system that relies on a server is affected by its move.

stem: During a cleanup change, an administrator at a ski resort disables an account that looks unused. The lift ticket scanners then stop validating passes, because they used that account to reach the pass database.
ask: Which of the following would have caught this before the change?

options.t: Scheduling the change at night
options.why: The scanners would fail whenever the account was disabled.

options.t: Mapping which systems used it
options.why: A dependency map would have shown that the scanners used the account.

options.t: Restarting the scanners afterward
options.why: A restart does not give the scanners a working account again.

options.t: Keeping the change in its approved scope
options.why: Disabling the account was the approved work; scope was not the problem.

detail: they used that account to reach the pass database
explain: Hidden dependencies cause surprising outages. Mapping what relies on a component before changing it finds them in time.

ask: Which of the following describes documentation as part of change management?

options.t: Keeping every change inside its approved scope
options.why: That describes restricted activities.

options.t: Tracking when a service is out of use
options.why: That describes downtime.

options.t: Keeping records in line with the setup after each change
options.why: Documentation means keeping records current so they match the environment after every change.

options.t: Listing old programs that lack vendor support
options.why: That describes identifying legacy applications.

explain: Documentation in change management keeps records, mainly network diagrams and policies or procedures, matching the environment after every change.

ask: When should records such as network maps and written steps be brought up to date for a change?

options.t: Once a year during the audit
options.why: Changes happen often, so a yearly update leaves records wrong for months.

options.t: Only after an incident exposes a gap
options.why: By then outdated records have already misled the people responding.

options.t: Whenever there is spare time
options.why: Updates left for spare time are easily forgotten.

options.t: As a step of the change itself
options.why: Documentation updates belong in the change process itself, so records never fall behind.

explain: Because changes happen often, documentation updates are built into each change instead of being left for later.

stem: A process analyst at a logistics company reviews its change checklist. It covers request, testing, approval, scheduling and implementation, but nothing makes anyone revise the network maps or runbooks once the work is done.
ask: Which change management step is missing from the checklist?

options.t: Approval process
options.why: The checklist already covers approval.

options.t: Documentation
options.why: Nothing in the checklist brings records up to date after the work, which is the documentation step.

options.t: Test results
options.why: The checklist already covers testing.

options.t: Maintenance window
options.why: The checklist already covers scheduling.

detail: nothing makes anyone revise the network maps or runbooks
explain: Documentation updates should be part of the change process itself; a checklist without them lets records drift from reality.

stem: During a malware outbreak at an engineering firm, responders lose an hour because their records still show servers that were retired in changes last year.
ask: Which change management practice would have prevented the lost hour?

options.t: Backout plan
options.why: A backout plan undoes a failed change; the retirements worked, the records were not updated.

options.t: Impact analysis
options.why: Impact analysis rates risk before a change; it does not keep records current afterward.

options.t: Documentation
options.why: Keeping records current after each change would have removed the retired servers.

options.t: Restricted activities
options.why: Nothing in the stem shows work outside an approved scope.

detail: their records still show servers that were retired
explain: Outdated documents mislead incident response. Updating records as part of each change keeps responders working from the real environment.

stem: A network manager at a law firm finds that, after the data center move, the network map still shows the old core switch, and the server restore runbook still names the old backup appliance.
ask: Which practice covers bringing both items up to date?

options.t: Updating diagrams
options.why: This would fix the network map, but not the restore runbook, and the stem asks about both.

options.t: Updating policies/procedures
options.why: This would fix the restore runbook, but not the network map, and the stem asks about both.

options.t: Version control
options.why: Version control keeps the history of files; it does not revise them to match the new setup.

options.t: Documentation
options.why: Documentation covers every record that must match the environment, including both the map and the runbook.

detail: the network map still shows the old core switch, and the server restore runbook
explain: Documentation is the umbrella: updating diagrams fixes pictures of the environment, updating procedures fixes instructions, and this move needs both.

stem: An auditor at a card processor finds that every revision of the firewall settings is stored with its author and date. The written firewall management steps, however, still describe the firewall that was replaced a year ago.
ask: Which practice did the change process leave out?

options.t: Documentation
options.why: The records were never brought in line with the new firewall, so documentation was left out.

options.t: Version control
options.why: Version control is working: every settings revision is stored with its author and date.

options.t: Test results
options.why: The stem raises no question about whether the change was tested.

options.t: Backout plan
options.why: The stem raises no question about undoing the change.

detail: still describe the firewall that was replaced a year ago
explain: Version control records how files changed, but it does not make written steps match the environment; that is the documentation step of each change.

stem: A security manager at a seaport writes a memo on why records must follow every change.
ask: Which of the following problems of outdated records should the memo name? (Select TWO)

options.t: Troubleshooters are misled about the current setup
options.why: Outdated documents mislead troubleshooting.

options.t: Services fail to restart after changes
options.why: Restart failures come from the systems themselves, not from records.

options.t: Old programs lose vendor support
options.why: Vendor support ends for its own reasons, not because records are stale.

options.t: Incident responders act on a wrong picture of the network
options.why: Outdated documents mislead incident response.

options.t: Approved changes take longer to schedule
options.why: Scheduling depends on the maintenance window, not on record accuracy.

detail: why records must follow every change
explain: Outdated documentation misleads both troubleshooting and incident response, which is why updates are part of every change.

stem: A compliance analyst at a regional telecom reviews the close-out record below.
ask: Which of the following problems does this record show?

options.t: Its work went outside the approved scope
options.why: Nothing in the record shows extra work.

options.t: It caused unplanned downtime
options.why: The record mentions no outage, and the tests passed.

options.t: Its records were left out of date
options.why: The map and runbook boxes are unchecked, yet the change was closed.

options.t: It had no way to be undone
options.why: The record says nothing about a backout plan.

detail: [ ] Network map revised
explain: A change is not complete until its documentation is current. Closing with the map and runbook unrevised leaves records that no longer match the network.

stem: A network engineer at a pet food maker argues that the change request record is all the documentation a change needs. Once a change closes, he says, the network map and the operating procedures can be left as they are.
ask: Which of the following explains why this is not enough?

options.t: Other records would no longer match the network
options.why: Documentation keeps every record matching the environment. A change request does not update the map or the procedures.

options.t: A change request cannot be stored for long
options.why: Change records are kept; the problem is that the map and procedures go stale.

options.t: Network maps must be redrawn every month
options.why: Maps are updated when a change alters them, not on a monthly timetable.

options.t: Procedures only matter during an audit
options.why: Staff and responders follow procedures every day, not only auditors.

detail: the network map and the operating procedures can be left as they are
explain: Documentation means keeping records, mainly diagrams and procedures, matching the environment after each change. A change request records the change; it does not keep the map or the procedures current.

stem: The IT manager at an industrial bakery learns that dozens of small changes were made this year, and some were closed without their records being updated. She wants to find which network maps and procedures no longer match what is running.
ask: Which of the following would show this?

options.t: A restore of older copies of the records
options.why: Restoring older copies brings back the same stale records; it does not show what changed in the environment.

options.t: A new impact analysis of each change
options.why: Impact analysis predicts the effects of a change before approval. It does not check records against what is running.

options.t: A check of the records against the live systems
options.why: Records must match the environment, so comparing them with what is really running shows which ones drifted.

options.t: A count of the changes made this year
options.why: A count says how many changes there were, not which records they left wrong.

detail: no longer match what is running
explain: Records drift when changes skip their documentation step. Checking them against what is really running, for example with discovery scans, finds the ones to update.

ask: Which of the following describes updating diagrams after a change?

options.t: Rewriting the step-by-step instructions staff follow
options.why: That is updating policies and procedures, which covers instructions rather than pictures.

options.t: Revising network drawings to show the current setup
options.why: Updating diagrams means revising network and system drawings so they show the architecture as it is now.

options.t: Listing the people a change will affect
options.why: That is identifying stakeholders.

options.t: Writing down how to undo a change that fails
options.why: That is a backout plan.

explain: Diagrams show how the environment is built and connected, so they are revised after each change that alters what they show.

ask: Which of the following explains why network drawings must be revised after a change?

options.t: They replace the need for a backout plan
options.why: A drawing shows the layout; it does not undo a failed change.

options.t: They guide troubleshooting and incident response
options.why: Diagrams are used in troubleshooting and incident response, so they must match reality.

options.t: They decide when a change may happen
options.why: When a change happens is set by the maintenance window.

options.t: They list who approved each change
options.why: Approvals are recorded by the approval process, not on network drawings.

explain: Diagrams must match reality because people troubleshoot and respond to incidents from them, and they are easy to forget.

stem: A network engineer at a vineyard moves the guest wireless network to a different switch and adds a link to the winery's second building. The way staff carry out their work does not change.
ask: Which documentation task does this change call for?

options.t: Updating policies/procedures
options.why: The stem says the way staff work does not change, so no instructions need revising.

options.t: Standard operating procedure
options.why: An SOP is a written routine; no routine task changes here.

options.t: Impact analysis
options.why: Impact analysis rates risk before approval; it is not a documentation task after the change.

options.t: Updating diagrams
options.why: A moved network and a new link change the layout, so the network drawings must be revised.

detail: adds a link to the winery's second building
explain: A change to how the network is laid out and connected calls for revised diagrams so they match the real architecture.

stem: A network technician at a hops farm spends a morning hunting for a slow link that the network map does not show. The link was added during a change in the spring.
ask: Which documentation task was skipped after the spring change?

options.t: Updating diagrams
options.why: The map was never revised to show the new link, so it did not match reality.

options.t: Updating policies/procedures
options.why: The problem is a missing link on the map, not outdated instructions.

options.t: Standard operating procedure
options.why: An SOP describes a routine task; the stem is about a picture of the network.

options.t: Backout plan
options.why: A backout plan undoes a failed change; the spring change worked.

detail: a slow link that the network map does not show
explain: Diagrams are used in troubleshooting and are easy to forget. Revising them after each change keeps them useful.

stem: During an outage at a regional airport, the network team opens the repository that stores its network drawings and finds only a drawing from two years ago. Several links were added since, and no one ever revised the drawing.
ask: Which of the following was missing?

options.t: Version control
options.why: The repository keeps its history; there was simply no newer drawing to store.

options.t: Backout plan
options.why: The outage is not about undoing a change; the team needs a current picture.

options.t: Updating diagrams
options.why: No one revised the drawing after the changes, so there was no current one to find.

options.t: Dependencies
options.why: The stem describes an out-of-date drawing, not systems relying on each other.

detail: no one ever revised the drawing
explain: Version control can only return versions that were made. If the diagram was never revised after the changes, the step that was missing is updating diagrams.

stem: A cloud engineer at a ticket reseller adds a nightly export of sales data to a partner's storage. The drawings that show where customer data flows are left as they were.
ask: Which risk does this create?

options.t: The export fails to restart each night
options.why: Stale drawings do not stop the export from running.

options.t: Staff follow outdated restore steps
options.why: Restore steps are procedures; the stem concerns drawings of data flows.

options.t: The export runs outside its maintenance window
options.why: Drawings have no effect on when the export runs.

options.t: Reviewers miss that data now leaves the company
options.why: The data flow drawings no longer show the new path, so anyone relying on them misses it.

detail: are left as they were
explain: Data flow diagrams are diagrams too. If they are not revised, people reviewing where data goes work from a wrong picture.

stem: A network administrator at a design school sorts this week's changes into those that need the network drawings revised and those that do not.
ask: Which of the following changes need the network drawings revised? (Select TWO)

options.t: Adding a link between two campus buildings
options.why: A new link changes how the network connects, so the drawings must show it.

options.t: Raising the password length for staff accounts
options.why: A password rule does not change the network layout.

options.t: Rewording the help desk's reset instructions
options.why: Instructions are procedures, not network drawings.

options.t: Moving the printers to a new subnet
options.why: Moving devices to another subnet changes the architecture the drawings show.

options.t: Renewing a web server certificate
options.why: A renewed certificate changes nothing about how the network is laid out.

detail: need the network drawings revised
explain: Diagrams are revised when a change alters what they show: links, subnets and where devices sit, not rules or instructions.

stem: A network analyst at a sugar refinery compares the revision date of the network map with the change log below.
ask: Which of the following left the network map out of date?

lines: 2026-06-19 CHG-640 moved VoIP phones to VLAN 30

options.t: Only the August change
options.why: A renewed certificate does not change the network layout.

options.t: The April and June changes
options.why: The April firewall was added before the map was revised in May, so the map already shows it.

options.t: Only the June change
options.why: Moving the phones to another VLAN changed the layout after the map's last revision.

options.t: All three changes
options.why: The April change is already on the May map, and the certificate renewal changes no layout.

detail: Network map NET-CORE: last revised 2026-05-01
explain: Only a layout change made after the map's last revision leaves it out of date. The April firewall came before the May revision, and a certificate renewal changes no layout.

stem: A security analyst at a cosmetics retailer must contain an infected laptop and asks for the network drawing to choose which link to cut.
ask: Which of the following must be true of the drawing for this to work?

options.t: It is stored with the laptop's backups
options.why: Where the drawing is stored does not make it accurate.

options.t: It shows the layout as it is today
options.why: Responders choose what to isolate from the drawing, so it must show the current network.

options.t: It shows only the internet links
options.why: The analyst needs the internal links too, to cut the right one.

options.t: It was approved by the change board long ago
options.why: An old approval says nothing about whether the drawing is current.

detail: to choose which link to cut
explain: Incident responders rely on diagrams to decide what to isolate, so diagrams that do not match reality send them the wrong way.

stem: An auditor at a freight airline asks for something showing how the cargo systems connect and where shipment data flows. The IT team offers its asset list of serial numbers and owners.
ask: What should the team provide instead?

options.t: The current network and data flow drawings
options.why: Diagrams show how systems connect and where data flows, which is what the auditor asked for.

options.t: A list of installed software releases
options.why: A list of software shows what is installed, not how systems connect.

options.t: The help desk's restore runbook
options.why: A runbook gives steps to follow, not connections or data flows.

options.t: The log of approved changes
options.why: A change log lists what changed, not how the systems connect now.

detail: how the cargo systems connect and where shipment data flows
explain: An inventory lists assets; a diagram shows how they connect and where data flows, and it must be kept current through every change.

ask: Which of the following describes updating policies and procedures after a change?

options.t: Revising written rules and steps for the new setup
options.why: This means revising policies and procedures so staff follow steps that fit the changed system or process.

options.t: Revising network drawings so they show the new layout
options.why: That is updating diagrams, which shows structure rather than instructions.

options.t: Keeping each earlier copy of changed files
options.why: That is version control, which keeps history rather than revising instructions.

options.t: Limiting implementers to the approved work
options.why: That is restricted activities.

explain: When a change alters how work is done, the written policies and procedures are revised so staff follow steps that fit the new system.

ask: Which of the following problems comes from step-by-step instructions that still describe a replaced system?

options.t: The system fails to restart
options.why: Outdated instructions do not stop a system from restarting.

options.t: The staff make errors or improvise
options.why: Stale procedures cause errors, and improvised steps can skip security checks.

options.t: The network drawing goes out of date
options.why: Drawings go out of date when they are not revised; that is a separate record.

options.t: The change goes beyond its approved scope
options.why: Scope is set by the approval, not by old instructions.

explain: Instructions written for a replaced system make staff fail or improvise, which is why revising them is part of closing a change.

stem: A payroll firm moves from an on-site time clock server to a cloud time tracking service. The payroll clerks' month-end checklist still tells them to export hours from the old server.
ask: Which documentation task did the change skip?

options.t: Updating diagrams
options.why: The problem is outdated instructions, not a drawing of the environment.

options.t: Backout plan
options.why: A backout plan undoes a failed change; the move worked.

options.t: Updating policies/procedures
options.why: The clerks' written steps still describe the old server, so the procedure was never revised.

options.t: Restricted activities
options.why: Nothing in the stem shows work outside the approved change.

detail: still tells them to export hours from the old server
explain: A new system often needs new procedures. A checklist that still points at the old server should have been revised as part of the change.

stem: A cruise terminal replaces its overhead paging system with a messaging app on staff phones. The project manager must make sure night staff know the new way to call a technician.
ask: Which of the following tells night staff the new way to call a technician?

options.t: A revised drawing of the paging network
options.why: A drawing shows how the network is built, not what staff should do.

options.t: A restored copy of the old paging settings
options.why: Restoring old settings undoes the change instead of telling staff how to work now.

options.t: A list of who approved the change
options.why: An approval list says nothing about how to call a technician.

options.t: A revised call-out procedure
options.why: Written instructions tell staff what to do with the new system.

detail: know the new way to call a technician
explain: Procedures are the written steps staff follow, so a change in how work is done means revising them.

stem: An auditor at a medical supply firm compares how the help desk actually sets up new laptops with the written setup steps. They differ, because the steps were never revised after a cloud enrollment service replaced the old imaging server.
ask: What will the auditor record?

options.t: A passed control, since a working method exists
options.why: A working method that differs from the written one is still a gap an auditor reports.

options.t: A finding that practice and documents do not match
options.why: Auditors compare practice with written procedure, so a stale procedure becomes a finding.

options.t: A dependency between the old and new systems
options.why: The issue is outdated written steps, not one system relying on another.

options.t: A backout of the enrollment service
options.why: An auditor records findings; nothing in the stem calls for undoing the new service.

detail: the steps were never revised after a cloud enrollment service replaced the old imaging server
explain: Auditors check practice against written procedure, so procedures not revised after a change turn into audit findings.

stem: A security engineer at a bus maker rewrites the remote access steps for a new VPN product and wants them in use the day the product goes live.
ask: Which of the following should happen before the new steps are published?

options.t: The old steps are deleted from version control
options.why: Old versions are kept in version control for audit history, not deleted.

options.t: The steps skip review since the engineer wrote them
options.why: Revised procedures go through the normal document review, whoever wrote them.

options.t: Their owner approves them through the usual review
options.why: Revised procedures go through the normal document review and are approved by their owner.

options.t: Staff are told nothing until problems arise
options.why: Affected staff are told when the new steps take effect, not after problems.

detail: wants them in use the day the product goes live
explain: Revised procedures are approved by their owners through normal document review, then published when the change goes live and shared with affected staff.

stem: A compliance officer at a credit union lists last month's changes and asks which ones changed how staff do their work.
ask: Which of the following changes call for revised written instructions? (Select TWO)

options.t: A new expense tool replacing an emailed form
options.why: Staff now file expenses a different way, so the instructions must change.

options.t: A failed disk replaced with the same model
options.why: A like-for-like part changes nothing about how staff work.

options.t: More memory added to the mail server
options.why: Staff use email the same way after a memory upgrade.

options.t: Visitor sign-in moved from a paper book to a tablet
options.why: Reception now signs visitors in differently, so the written steps must change.

options.t: A switch port label renamed
options.why: A renamed label does not change how staff do their work.

detail: changed how staff do their work
explain: Procedures are revised when a change alters how people do their work; changes that leave the work the same need no new instructions.

stem: An incident handler at a regional radio network opens the runbook below. The log server it names was retired last spring, and account management moved to a cloud directory.
ask: What is the risk of this runbook in its current state?

lines: Step 1: Pull sign-in logs from logsrv01.example

options.t: The log server restarts during an incident
options.why: The log server was retired; it cannot restart.

options.t: The account is blocked by the deny list
options.why: No deny list is involved; the steps themselves are outdated.

options.t: The network map goes out of date
options.why: The runbook is a procedure; its age does not change the map.

options.t: The responders lose time on steps that fail
options.why: Steps 1 and 2 point at a retired server and an old console, so responders waste time during an incident.

detail: The log server it names was retired last spring
explain: An incident runbook pointing at a retired server costs time when it matters most, which is why procedures are revised as part of each change.

stem: The security office manager at a university replaces the badge printing software. The rule that every badge shows a photo stays the same.
ask: Which of the following needs revising?

options.t: The front desk's guide for making badges
options.why: The new software changes how badges are made, so the front desk's procedure must be revised.

options.t: The rule that badges show a photo
options.why: The stem says the photo rule stays the same.

options.t: The list of change board members
options.why: The change does not alter who sits on the board.

options.t: The backout plan of last year's change
options.why: A past change's backout plan is not affected by this one.

detail: The rule that every badge shows a photo stays the same
explain: A policy states the rule and a procedure states the steps. Here the rule stays the same while the steps change, so the procedure is what gets revised.

stem: The warehouse manager at a distribution center replaces the handheld scanners with ones that use a different sign-in. The revised scanning steps are published.
ask: What should the manager do so the change takes hold?

options.t: Keep the old steps posted beside the revised ones
options.why: Old steps for retired scanners invite errors.

options.t: Wait for errors before telling anyone
options.why: Waiting for errors means staff fail first; they should be told when the change goes live.

options.t: Brief and train staff on the revised steps
options.why: Affected staff are told about the new steps, and trained when how they work changes.

options.t: Revise only the network map
options.why: A map does not teach staff the new sign-in.

detail: use a different sign-in
explain: Publishing revised procedures is not enough on its own: affected staff are told, and trained when their work changes.

ask: Which of the following describes version control?

options.t: Tracking each change to files with who, what and when
options.why: Version control records every change over time, with who changed what and when, so earlier versions can be compared or restored.

options.t: Deciding whether a proposed change may be made at all

options.t: Revising drawings to match the network

options.t: Planning how to undo a failed change

ask: Which practice keeps a history of every edit to a set of scripts, with the author and time of each?

options.t: Updating diagrams

options.t: Impact analysis

options.t: Version control

stem: A web administrator at a cereal maker finds that the shop's checkout page broke after one of three edits made to its settings file this week. She needs to see what each edit changed and who made it.
ask: Which of the following practices gives the administrator this?

options.t: Backout plan
options.why: A backout plan says how to undo a change; it does not show what each edit changed or who made it.

options.t: Version control
options.why: It stores each edit with its author and lets two versions be compared to see what changed.

options.t: Updating diagrams
options.why: Diagrams show how systems connect, not the edits to a settings file.

options.t: Impact analysis
options.why: Impact analysis predicts risk before a change; it does not record edits afterward.

detail: see what each edit changed and who made it
explain: Comparing versions of a file and seeing who changed it is the core of version control, which makes finding a bad edit quick.

stem: A network analyst at a county court compares a core router's running configuration with the last approved copy in the repository. She finds two lines that appear in no approved copy or change record.
ask: Which practice made this comparison possible?

options.t: Updating diagrams
options.why: Drawings show how the network connects, not the router's exact lines.

options.t: Version control
options.why: Keeping approved copies in a repository is what lets the running configuration be compared with them.

options.t: Restricted activities
options.why: The extra lines may break the scope limit, but that rule did not make the comparison possible.

options.t: Test results
options.why: Test results come from trying a change before rollout, not from comparing running settings later.

detail: the last approved copy in the repository

stem: Thirty minutes into a change at a payroll processor, new load balancer settings cause errors. The network engineer pulls the settings file from before the change out of the team's repository and puts it back.
ask: Which of the following BEST describes what supplied the earlier settings file?

options.why: Putting the old settings back is the backout, but the stem asks what supplied the earlier file.

options.t: Updating diagrams
options.why: Diagrams show layout; they hold no settings files.

options.t: Test results

options.t: Version control

detail: out of the team's repository

explain: Version control supports backout plans: the plan says to restore the previous state, and version control supplies the exact earlier file.

stem: An office manager at a design studio proposes using the studio's version control system as the backup for the whole file server, including the client photo archive.
ask: Which of the following is the flaw in the proposal?

options.t: It keeps only what someone deliberately commits
options.why: Version control stores the revisions people commit; it does not copy everything on the server the way a backup does.

options.t: It can store only one earlier copy of a file
options.why: It keeps the whole history, not a single earlier copy.

options.t: It records changes without the author or time

options.t: It cannot restore an earlier version

explain: Version control records deliberate revisions of code, configurations and documents. It is not a backup of a whole server's data.

options.why: Approval comes from the change process, not from storing files.

options.t: No downtime during configuration changes

options.why: Any earlier version can be restored, which supports backout plans.

options.t: Automatic updates of the network drawings

options.why: Each laptop holds every revision, not only the newest one.
